stem: Ilse set up a business 5 years ago as a sole trader importing foods from Eastern Europe and supplying small delicatessens. Last year she wished to expand her business but needed more capital, therefore she involved her brother Werner and persuaded him to invest in her business. In order to do so, he insisted that the business should be re-organised into a corporate structure and that he would then subscribe for shares. Werner also insisted that his two sons Dieter and Karl should be appointed as directors. Ilse was content with this, therefore The Eastern Food Co. Ltd. was incorporated with an issued share capital of 100,001 shares at £1 each. Werner subscribed for 50,000 shares and paid £25,000 with the further £25,000 being left unpaid. Ilse had her existing business valued at £50,000 by independent experts and then sold the business to the newly incorporated company in exchange for 50,000 shares. Ilse's daughter Ursula subscribed for the remaining 1 share and paid £1. Ilse, Dieter and Karl were named as first directors. Ursula dealt with the administration of the business but held no office in the company. Ilse has been used to making all the decisions for the business on her own and she finds it difficult to have Dieter and Karl interfering all the time. She consults you as to her rights and responsibilities in the company and wants to know in particular who is responsible for the management of the company.
ask: Which one of the following best summarises the correct advice?

options.en: Ilse and Werner have the final say in all decisions concerning the management of the company because they hold most of the shares. If Ursula were to cast a vote in support of either of the two, then that resolution would pass
Dieter and Karl and Ilse are all responsible for the management of the company as they are all directors

Dieter, Karl and Ilse are responsible for the management of the company in consultation with all the shareholders. Because Ilse is both a shareholder and a director, she would have the final say on all decisions
Dieter, Karl and Ilse are all responsible for the management of the company, subject to a requirement to consult with the majority shareholders
The shareholders and directors of the company are legally responsible for the management of the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is [B]. The Companies Act 2006 places the legal power and duty for the management of the company with the directors. It is possible for the articles of association of a company to reserve certain matters to the shareholders in a general meeting and employment legislation requires companies to consult employees on certain issues. The facts do not imply that the articles of association reserve such powers to the shareholders.

stem: Susan, Madeleine and Leigh are shareholders in Swift Cars South London Ltd, which is a small family business. Susan is a director and their friend Peter is also a director. The business employs three members of staff. The articles of association set out details of the management structure. The directors Susan and Peter wish to make some changes which are currently prohibited by the articles.
ask: Can this be done and if so how?

options.en: Susan and Peter can make the changes as they are directors
Susan, Madeleine and Leigh can make the changes as long as they all agree
The articles would need to be amended and this can be done long as all the shareholders agree
The articles would need to be amended and this could be done by a vote in favour of the resolution by 75% of the shareholders' votes
The articles would need to be amended and this could be done by a vote from the majority of shareholders

explanation.en: The correct answer is [D]. As we are told that the changes the directors wish to make are prohibited by the articles, the directors must ask the shareholders to amend the articles. Directors can not overrule anything in the articles. A change in the articles of a company requires a special resolution, which means a minimum of 75% of the shareholders' votes.

stem: Stan, David and Marlene run a business called "Millennium Car Co," Stan is the only shareholder. Business decisions are all made by Stan and David, but David and Marlene are involved in the day to day management of the business. The business is registered with the Companies House.
ask: Who would be liable if the business goes into liquidation and is unable to pay its debts?

options.en: Stan because he is the only shareholder
Stan and David because they made all the business decisions
David and Marlene because they dealt with the day to day management of the business
No one would be responsible other than the company because the company has a separate legal personality
David because he was involved in both the business decisions and the day to day management

explanation.en: The correct answer is [A]. Although, we know from the question that the business is a company and does have a separate legal personality, we can deduce that the company is not limited company, because its name does not end with the words Limited Company or Ltd., which is an obligatory requirement for a limited company. The consequence is that the shareholders liability is not limited to the unpaid portion of their shares, as would be the case if the company were limited. Stan is the only shareholder, therefore he would be liable. Most businesses that operate as companies do run as limited companies, but there are a few who choose to run as unlimited companies. It is important to be aware when dealing with a company, whether it is limited or not.

stem: The Eastern Food Co Ltd. is managed by Olga and Jan who are both directors. The shareholders are Chris and Katherine who each owns 50% of the shares. Chris sells half his shares to Olga and then dies.
ask: Who is now responsible for running the business?

options.en: Katherine is responsible because she is the majority shareholder
Katherine and Olga are responsible because they are the only living shareholders
Katherine and Olga are responsible together with the executor or administrator of Chris' estate
Olga and Jan are responsible because they are directors
Olga is responsible because she is both a shareholder and a director

explanation.en: The correct answer is [D]. The directors are legally responsible for the running of a company. t is irrelevant if a shareholder dies. Unless the articles of a company prove otherwise, it i rrelevant that a director is also a shareholder and as such a director would have no greate authority in the company than any other director.

stem: Encordia Ltd. has just been acquired by Henry and Joseph, who hold the shares in trust for a syndicate of investors that wishes to remain anonymous. You have been asked by them and the existing directors to look closely at their company structure and paper work to ensure that everything is as it should be, and to identify any serious legal problems.
ask: Which of the following matters identifies an issue which should be amended by the company?

options.en: Encordia Ltd. Is using a fleet of cars that do not belong to Encordia
A company secretary has not been appointed
The business premises, which are owned by Encordia Ltd. have been insured in the names of the shareholders
The company bank account has two signatories. A signature from either is sufficient and one of those signatories does not need to be a director
The articles of the company allow the shareholders to overrule any decision of the directors, as long as a minimum of 51% of the shareholders who vote are in favour of the resolution

explanation.en: The correct answer is [C]. The company owns the property, therefore it is the one to have an insurable interest and not the shareholders. All the other points above are legitimate business practices and within the law.

stem: Johan and Janet subscribed for shares in a new venture Fit 4 Life Ltd. The issued share capital of the new company was 100,001 with a nominal value of £1 each. Johan subscribed for 20,000 shares and paid £5,000, the remainder being unpaid. Janet subscribed for 30,000 and paid £10,000, the remainder being unpaid. This capital was spent on purchasing machinery and paying advance rent for premises. After a period of 12 months the company went into insolvent liquidation owing £40,000 to a variety of creditors.
ask: What is the liability of Johan and Janet?

options.en: They are not liable for any of the debts because the business was a limited company
Johan is liable to contribute £15,000 and Janet is liable to contribute £20,000. These amounts are to be paid to the company liquidator
Johan is liable to pay up to £15,000 to creditors and Janet must pay creditors up to £20,000. The creditors can claim from whichever of the two they choose to claim from
Because Janet had subscribed for 30,000 shares and Johan for 20,000 shares they are liable on a ratio of 3:2 and for every £2 Johan contributes Janet must contribute £3

Because Johan had £15,000 outstanding on his shares and Janet had £20,000 outstanding, they must contribute to creditors on a ratio of 3:4 and for every £3 that Johan contributes Janet must contribute £4

explanation.en: The correct answer is [B]. Johan is liable to contribute £15,000 and Janet is liable to contribute £20,000. These amounts are to be paid to the company liquidator. Where a limited company goes into liquidation, the shareholders' liability is limited to the unpaid portion on their shares. It is irrelevant if one of the shareholders has no funds to pay the liability, the remaining shareholders liability remains limited to the unpaid portion on their shares, even if the company is wound up and cannot pay its creditors in full from the funds that are left. The members' liability is, therefore, limited to paying to the company the full value of their shares.

stem: Property Direct Plc. was set up by Peter and William in 2008 with each subscribing for an equal number of shares and paying out only the minimum permitted by law for such a venture. They are the only shareholders. When the business goes into liquidation the assets of the business are insufficient to pay the debts.
ask: Which of the following best describes Peter and William's liability with regards to the debts?

options.en: They are not liable as the company has a separate legal personality
They are liable for the whole debts because the company was a Plc and they did not secure public investment
Peter and William are each liable for half of the outstanding debts
Peter and William have joint and severable liability for the debt, because they started the company together and although it is named as a Plc they never secured public investment
Peter and William are liable to the extent of the unpaid portion of their shares

explanation.en: The correct answer is [E]. In the case of a limited company, whether it is public or private, shareholders liability is limited to the unpaid portion of their shares. We know from this question that the company is public as it has the suffix Plc. Both Peter and William put down the minimum amount of money permitted by law for such a venture, but each subscribed for half of the shares. The minimum issued share capital for a Plc is currently £50,000 and the law requires that one quarter must be paid. Consequently, we know that Peter and William only put in £6,250 each. They each have an unpaid portion of their shares and are liable to the extent of that unpaid portion.

stem: Your client is considering to incorporate a new legal entity for his business and asks for your advice as to the correct procedures in Companies House.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe the correct legal position?

options.en: A public company may have a company secretary
A private company may commence business before Companies House has issued a certificate of incorporation
A secretary of a private company can also be a sole director
A private company may not dispense with the need to hold meetings of its members
A secretary of a public company cannot also hold office as a director

explanation.en: The best answer is C. A secretary of a private company can also be a sole director. Option A is incorrect as a public company must (as opposed to 'may') have a secretary. Option B is incorrect as a private company may commence business as soon as Companies House has issued a certificate of incorporation, but not before. Option D is incorrect - a private company may decide to not hold any meetings of its members; Option E is also incorrect, as there is no legal impediment in appointing a director of a public company as the company secretary.

stem: Comfort Zone Ltd. owns and manages a chain of bed and breakfast hotels in South East England. The shareholders are Michaela, Samuel, Investment Property Ltd. and Hammorabi LLP. The directors are David, Susan, Harry and Henrietta. The practice has been for each director to manage one property, although they do not attend the hotels under their management on a daily basis. Hotel staff are employed, including a duty hotel manager for each premises. One of the hotels, in error, allows a large group of guests to double book and consequently is unable to accommodate them upon arrival. The guests secure alternative accommodation at short notice, but have to pay a much higher rate.
ask: Who is liable legally for the loss of the guests which resulted from the breach of contract of the hotel?

options.en: The director who was responsible for the hotel premises where the error occurred
All the directors are jointly liable because they represent the company and have legal authority to bind it
The shareholders are liable but only to the extent of any unpaid portion on their shares
Comfort Zone Ltd. is liable together with the duty manager of the hotel where the error occurred
Comfort Zone Ltd. is liable

explanation.en: The correct answer is [E]. The company has a separate legal personality and is bound by the acts of its directors. The company is liable for the consequences of the mistakes of its directors including the mistakes of staff employed by the company when they carry out their duties as an employee. The company is the relevant legal person.

stem: Simon ran a business printing logos on sports clothing and equipment. He operated initially as a sole trader. He then set up a company S.P. Ltd. and sold his business to the company in exchange for the total issued share capital of 50,000 shares of a nominal value of £1 each. His business had been independently valued at £70,000 prior to the sale and consequently Simon specifically excluded a range of plant and machinery from the sale agreement. He then leased the plant and machinery to the company for an agreed fee. Simon also leant the company a further £10,000 needed to purchase new computer equipment and software. Simon acquired a charge of the equipment as security against the loan. For various reasons the company failed and owed money to a number of creditors. Simon wishes to know
ask: How much, if any, of his investment in the business would be returned to him?

options.en: Simon can not recover any of his investment until all other creditors have been paid

Simon can recover the plant and machinery that he leased to the, but will have to wait for the other creditors to be paid before he can recover his loan, because he is not an independent bona fide shareholder and therefore the company is a sham
Simon can recover the plant and machinery that he leased to the company because he is still the owner of them. He can also recover his £10,000 loan or seize the equipment over which he has a charge

It would be an affront to the law to allow Simon to recover anything until all other creditors have been paid in full because the incorporation of the company was a mere scheme to allow Simon to continue business with the benefit of limited liability
Simon would be able to recover a portion of the £10,000 loan that he gave to the company on a pro-rata basis with other creditors when the company is wound up

explanation.en: The correct answer is [C]. The principle of a separate legal personality was clearly confirmed by the House of Lords (now the UK Supreme Court) in the leading case of Salomon. It is irrelevant that the shareholder is a sole shareholder or that he sold his own business to the company that he then managed in exactly the same way as he had managed his business. The law of England and Wales permits this activity and therefore the company is a separate legal entity from Simon, the sole shareholder. Consequently, in the case of liquidation, Simon stands as any other creditor and recovers as such money that he leant to the company or equipment leased to the company. He can not recover his share capital until such time as all creditors have been fully paid.

stem: A limited company is unable to pay its debts. A liquidator is being appointed. He considers whether the activity of the directors was one of wrongful trading or whether it was fraudulent trading.
ask: The liquidator wishes to know what would need to be established to show wrongful trading Which of the following would best fit your advice?

options.en: The liquidator would need to establish that the directors allowed the company to continue trading even though it was making a loss
The liquidator would need to show that the directors knew on balance that insolvent liquidation was inevitable

The liquidator would need to show on balance that the directors continued to allow the company to trade beyond a time when they knew, or aught to have ascertained, that insolvent liquidation was inevitable
The liquidator would need to show on balance that the directors continued to trade with intent to defraud the company's creditors
The liquidator would need to show that on balance that the directors traded without the permission of the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is [C]. The wrongful trading provisions are included in section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986. There is no requirement to show any intent to defraud.

stem: Having completed her training Samantha left her employment with Beauty is us Ltd. and set up a business of her own. When she had joined Beauty is us Ltd. five years earlier she had been taken on as a trainee. She had agreed that if she completed her training with the company and then left at any time she would not solicit the company's clients, or set up in practice in the beauty business within a five mile radius of Beauty is us Ltd., for a period of two years from leaving the company. Samantha set up a company Lovely Lilies Ltd. and commenced to advertise the beauty therapy services of the new company. Her company operates within just over a two mile radius of Beauty is us Ltd. Samantha is the only shareholder of Lovely Lilies Ltd. and she is a sole director. Lovely Lilies Ltd. has especially targeted the women Samantha had catered for when she worked at Beauty is us Ltd.
ask: Can Beauty is us Ltd. prevent Samantha from reneging on her agreement with them?

options.en: Samantha is not reneging on her agreement with Beauty is us Ltd. Lovely Lilies Ltd. is a separate legal entity from Samantha and has made no agreement with Beauty is us
Although Samantha is reneging on her agreement, she can not be prevented from doing so because she has been clever enough to do so through the vehicle of a limited company
Beauty is us Ltd would only be able to have a legal remedy if they could show that Samantha was acting fraudulently

Beauty is us Ltd could seek to enforce the agreement with Samantha even though she is acting through a limited company. The court would need to be satisfied that the corporate vehicle was being used as a device to enable Samantha to escape her legal obligations
Because Samantha is the sole shareholder and sole director, Lovely Lilies Ltd. can not enjoy the benefit of separate personality

explanation.en: The correct answer is [D]. The courts may lift the veil of incorporation and treat a business as if it were run by individual members, if the court is satisfied that the company is being used as a device to escape legal obligations. Gilford Motor Company Ltd. v Horne (1933) demonstrates the point.

stem: Paul Burt is a sole shareholder in Paul Burt Ltd. The company provides management consultancy services. Paul Burt is a sole director. The Company employs two people; Paul Burt, who provides management consultancy services to the company's clients; and Sally Burt whose role is to deal with office administration. Several months after it began its operation, the company was forced to go into liquidation. One of the company's creditors, Techno Crarp Ltd. is owed a large sum and seeks your advice on whether his company can enforce against Paul Burt personally. Your client knows that Paul Burt owns a large house in Surrey and always drives a new car.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The shareholders of a company can never be held liable for the acts of a company, in light of the decision in the case of Salomon concerning a separate legal personality
A creditor can enforce a debt against a sole shareholder, where the creditor is satisfied that the company is being used as a device to enable the sole shareholder to escape his legal obligations
The courts can lift the veil of incorporation, if it is overwhelmingly in the interest of justice to do so
The courts must lift the veil of incorporation where it appears that the company is being used as a device to enable a person to escape its legal obligations
The courts may lift the veil of incorporation where it appears that the company is being used as a device to enable a person to escape its legal obligations

explanation.en: The correct answer is [E]. A creditor would not be able to enforce against a shareholder unless a court has lifted the veil and made an order against that named shareholder. The courts are not obliged to lift the veil of incorporation and the case law to date leaves some degree of uncertainty as to when the courts will do so. However, the situation outlined [E] shows that the courts have been known to lift the veil on occasions.

stem: Catering Direct Ltd. provided catering services at short notice to the business community. Peter was the sole shareholder. The company operated well and made reasonable profits. It also borrowed money and had some trade creditors. Peter died leaving one daughter. He had made no will.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position with regards to the company?

options.en: The company continues to exist until such time as it is wound up and is struck from the register of companies
The businesses corporate status will lapse by operation of law, as there are now no live shareholders
The business automatically passes to the beneficiaries of the deceased shareholders estate, who now own all the assets and liabilities of the business
The official receiver would be required to wind up the business, so that the company would cease to exist
Ownership of the company would pass to the main creditor of the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. One of the benefits of the corporate form is perpetual succession. It means that the company continues to exist notwithstanding death, bankruptcy or insanity of any or all of the shareholders. Option C is incorrect, as neither the business nor the shares of the company will automatically pass to the beneficiaries. When a member of the company dies, the right to his interest in the shares will pass to his beneficiaries under his will or intestacy. The rights of the deceased member will be administered by his personal representative, and will be subject to the provisions of the company's articles of association.

stem: Alison wishes to set up her own hair salon business. She has a small amount of capital. Her family home is owned by her husband who provides for all of the family needs. Alison would like to involve her sister Martha in the venture, but Martha, although she is interested and is a talented beauty therapist, is not a risk taker and is not very good at making business decisions. Alison is unsure how long the venture might last and whilst she is willing to risk her money, she still likes to withdraw it without complications whenever she needs it.
ask: Which of the following best suits her venture goals?

options.en: Alison should set up as a limited company because she will have the benefit of limited liability
Alison should commence business as a sole trader and invite her sister to work in the business as an employee only
Alison should set up business as a partnership with her sister Martha. Alison can take responsibility for the business side of the enterprise
Alison should set up business as an unlimited company because the business will enjoy the benefit of separate legal personality and can therefore hold assets in its own name
Alison should set up business with Martha as a limited liability partnership

explanation.en: The correct answer is [B]. Alison has expressed a wish to keep the business as simple as possible, which would suggest a sole trader model. Her circumstances do not suggest the need to protect her personal assets, which would be achieved by using a limited liability model, either an LLP or Ltd. By commencing as a sole trader her business can run flexibly and she would be able to wind up the business at any time without the complications that would be involved if she were to run it as a limited company. As a sole trader she will also not incur the trouble and expense of filing requirements with Companies House.

stem: Your client, David, wants to incorporate a private company for his business.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: David cannot register a private company if he is the only shareholder
If David is the company's secretary, he cannot be a director of the company
The company cannot begin to trade until it has a certificate of registration. Any purported attempt to trade prior to this would incur personal liability on David
A company cannot trade until it has its certificate of incorporation. Any purported attempt to trade prior to this would be fraudulent and incur criminal sanctions
A company can not be registered with less than £50,000 issued share capital

explanation.en: The correct answer is [C]. A company can not begin to trade until it has a certificate of incorporation. However, it frequently happens in practice that an entrepreneur will commence trading pending the issue of the certificate of registration. It would be wrong to commence such trading under any pretence that the company has already been incorporated, but that would not necessarily be fraudulent.

stem: Rita has been approached by her friend Bob to undertake a business venture with him, selling small but luxury sailing boats. They want to keep the business affairs of the venture as private as possible. Rita has decided to allow her trading company R Seines Holdings Ltd. to commence the venture with Bob. Rita is a director and majority shareholder in R Seines Holdings Ltd. Rita and Bob decide to form a limited liability partnership and Ian, Bob's 18 year old son, has asked and been allowed to be a partner. Because of lan's young age and lack of business experience it is agreed that he will not be permitted to make any business decisions without the agreement of the other partners. Ian's function is to deal with customers. Ian is allowed to attend partner meetings and voice his opinion. A customer of the business who dealt with Ian is unhappy about his purchase and says he will sue lan. Ian is worried because he has received a large inheritance from his great grandmother and does not wish to lose any of it. The customer knows that Ian is a wealthy young man.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The business can not legally operate as a partnership because one of the purported partners is a company. Consequently Ian would be liable as if he had acted as a sole trader

As long as the business was registered with Companies House in the proper form as a limited liability partnership, the partners who are natural persons, i.e. Ian and Bob, will be liable only to the extent of their investment in the business
Ian can not be liable because he never took part in decision making in the business
The limited liability partnership is liable for any loss or damage caused or any breach of contract. Ian's liability is limited to his investment in the business

The limited liability partnership is liable for any loss or damage caused or any breach of contract. Although Ian was named as a partner, because he was not allowed to make any decisions on his own he was not a true partner and therefore can not be liable for any loss

explanation.en: The correct answer is [D]. It is perfectly lawful for a company to be a partner in a limited liability partnership and this is a business model that does exist. A corporate partner would enjoy the same benefits of limited liability within such a partnership as any natural human partner i.e. liability limited to the extent of investment in the partnership. It is lawful for a partnership agreement to limit the powers of one or other partner so long as the agreement does not set out so many restrictions as to negate the character of a partnership. It is not uncommon in practice for a partner to have restrictions placed on their involvement in the management of the business.

stem: Sarah and Anne are animal lovers and set up a business together providing animal rescue services for abandoned and ill-treated cats and dogs. They are both women of independent means and don't charge for their services, although they accept donations. Their venture is supported by a few wealthy elderly philanthropist animal lovers and succeeds in covering its costs and keeps Sarah and Anne meaningfully occupied. Occasionally the venture runs at a profit and while also losses are made from time to time.
ask: Which of the following best describes Sarah and Anne's business relationship?

options.en: There is no partnership if the venture is not a business set up with a view to profit
There is a partnership at will even though there is no written agreement. They have occasionally made profits and therefore they fit the statutory definition in the Partnership Act 1890
There is no partnership because the two never discussed it. Even though a written agreement is not a requirement there must be an express oral agreement for a partnership
There is a partnership at will and the philanthropists who supplied funds have become partners by operation of law even though they may not realise this

There is a partnership at will because profits have occasionally been made. The philanthropists who occasionally supplied funds would be treated as limited partners, as they did not take part in the running of the business

explanation.en: The correct answer is [A]. It is essential that the business is managed with a view to profit in order for a partnership to exist. It is clear from the scenario that profits were never intended and were only occasionally incidental to the business.

stem: Gaston, Emanuel and Henry set up a business together writing specialised computer software for commercial clients. Gaston invests the sum of £10,000 in the business. Emanuel contributes a range of computer equipment to the current value of £10,000. Henry contributes premises currently valued at £30,000. Notwithstanding the fact that they have contributed a different value to the partnership assets, it is agreed that they will share profits equally as Henry does not expect to be able to contribute the same level of expertise and professional skills in the business. The partnership is registered as Soft Select LLP. After 5 years of trading the partners decide to wind up the business for various reasons related to their personal health. After calling in all debts and paying all liabilities the partnership has £30,000 in cash. The computer equipment that Emanuel contributed is valued at £100 and computer equipment that the company has recently purchased is valued at £5,000. The premises contributed by Henry are valued at £100,000.
ask: What will the partners be entitled on dissolution of the partnership?

options.en: Because the partners agreed to share profits equally they will each be entitled to one third of the assets on dissolution after they have been paid their capital entitlement
The partners will be entitled to distribution of the assets in the same ratio as the original value of their contribution, i.e. 1:1:3
The partners will be entitled to distribution of the assets in the same ratio as the current value of their original contribution, i.e. 1:300:1,000
The property valued at £100,000 will go back to Henry and the remaining partnership assets will be divided in equal share between the other two partners
Emanuel will be entitled to the current value of all computer equipment, Gaston will be entitled to all liquid cash and Henry will be entitled to the value of the premises

explanation.en: The correct answer is [A]. Unless the partners have agreed otherwise, following return of their capital entitlement, they would be entitled to distribution on dissolution in the same ratio as their entitlement to profits. If assets have appreciated or depreciated in value, the partners will share equally in the gain or loss.

stem: Dylan and Keith are partners providing accountancy services. They have known each other for many years and never had a formal partnership agreement drafted because they trusted each other. They started up the business twenty years ago with nothing but their professional expertise. They have built up a thriving practice and employ twelve people, eight of whom are professional staff. Dylan has discovered that Keith has received a substantial payment privately from a firm that is not a client of their practice. On further investigation he has discovered that this payment was made for business consultancy services provided by Keith during a period that he had taken annual leave. Dylan confronted Keith but Keith's response was to tell Dylan to mind his own business. Keith claims that he did the work in his own time without Dylan's support, using his own equipment and facilities and therefore he was entitled to do so. He further claims that because the firm he did the work for was not a client of the partnership, he was in the clear. Dylan has responded that from now on he will not discuss with Keith any business deals. Notwithstanding the disagreement, the two partners still wish to continue in business together and have found that they need each others respective skills and contacts in order to thrive. They want to regularise the position with regard to the private contract that Keith undertook, but more importantly they both wish to know clearly what they are allowed to do.
ask: Which of the following is the best advice you can give the partners, taking into account they wish to continue with their business?

options.en: Keith is entitled to carry out work outside the partnership as long as he does not use partnership resources and does not solicit partnership clients
The two partners should draw up an agreement making it clear that their partnership does not prevent them from carrying out work in competition with the partnership

Because of the partnership relationship Keith and Dylan have there is a duty not to deceive each other and they must not lie about matters concerning the business. However they are not obliged to volunteer information to each other
The law permits each partner to carry out business outside the partnership if such business is not competing with the partnership and does not use partnership property, name or customers
Because Keith made a secret profit, not permitted under partnership law, he must account to the partnership 50% of the profits that he made

explanation.en: The correct answer is [D]. The law permits each partner to carry out business outside the partnership if such business is not competing with the partnership and does not use partnership property, name or customers. However, it is possible for a partnership agreement to specifically provide that partners must dedicate all of their time diligently to partnership business and not pursue any business outside the partnership. Answer B is not the best option. While it is always advisable to have an agreement between the partners, there is an established law with respect to partners carrying out a business non-competing with the firm.

stem: Silas is a partner in a firm of accountants called Calc U Late. The firm consists of four partners: Philip, Silas, Emily and Tryhit. A scam has been uncovered and it seems that unbeknown to the other partners, Tryhit has accepted payment for non existent consultancy services supposedly provide by the firm. Silas is now being pursued through legal action for losses incurred as a result of fraud.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Silas can not be held liable for the fraud as he was not a party to it
Silas may be held liable for the fraud as it was conducted by his partner through the medium of the partnership and in the normal course of partnership activities
Silas is liable for fraud because it was committed by his partner and partners are always jointly and severally liable for the act of their partners
Silas can not be made liable for the fraud because he did not specifically authorise the act
Silas can not be made liable for fraud because Tryhit did not inform him and therefore Tryhit is in breach of his duty of utmost good faith

explanation.en: The correct answer is [B]. Partners can be held liable for the acts of their partners where the partner is acting in the scope of the normal partnership activities, in this case the purported provision of consultancy services by a firm of accountants. This would not be the case if a fraud was committed outside the scope of normal partnership activities.

ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position with regards to limited liability partnerships?

options.en: In a limited liability partnership each partner is jointly and severally liable to the other partners
If a limited liability partnership were to go into liquidation, each partner could be made liable to the full extent of his personal assets
In a limited liability partnership the partners are the ones who would be assessed for tax

In a limited liability partnership any partner who does not take part in the management of the company and only contributes capital would have his liability limited to the amount that he invests in the business
A limited liability partnership must be registered with Companies House together with a copy of the membership agreement

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. In a limited liability partnership the partners are the ones who would be assessed for tax. Although an LLP is required to be registered with Companies House, there is no requirement to submit a copy of the membership agreement.

stem: "Quality Build South East" provides building and repair services to consumers in South East England. The name "Quality Build South East" is the official name of the business and appears on all business correspondence. Peter runs the business which he started 10 years ago. 4 years ago he needed further capital for the business and Bob gave him £20,000 on condition that he, Bob should take on some of the work and management of the business. The business is now thriving and employs four other members of staff.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal definition of the business?

options.en: Peter is a sole trader running the business because Bob only joined the firm after it had began trading
The business is a company because there is more than one person involved in the management and the business employs other people
The business is a partnership because the two are working together
The business is a partnership because both men contributed money to set up and run the business
The business is a partnership because the two men agreed to run the business together and have already began to do so

explanation.en: [E] is correct. Peter was originally a sole trader. However, when he and Bob agreed that Bob would join him in the business and also be involved in management they created a partnership by oral agreement. Although it is preferable for business partners to have a partnership agreement drafted, there is no legal requirement for a written agreement.

stem: Phillip and Sons is a business supplying sports clothing and equipment to schools. Greg has been in business for over 50 years and his two sons and one daughter have grown up in the business and have all taken on various management responsibilities. They have all run the business together for years, but because it is a family business and they trust each other they never put anything in writing. Greg sadly dies at the age of 96.
ask: What is the legal position with regards to the business?

options.en: Greg's two sons now own the business because the name declared that it was Phillip and sons. Greg's daughter is not entitled to the business, but if the family wish they may continue to include her in the business
The law provides that the business should continue to be managed by the three remaining managers as long as it is solvent
The business was a partnership and because one of the partners has died, the legal position is that the partnership will lapse
The business was a sole trader. Now that Greg has died the business must be wound up
Although the daughter and two sons ran the business with Greg, it was not a lawful partnership as there was no written agreement. The business must be wound up now that Greg has died

explanation.en: The correct answer is [C]. Although it is preferable for a partnership agreement to be set out in writing, there is no legal requirement for this. When there is no agreement to the contrary such partnership is a partnership at will and is governed by the Partnership Act 1890. Although in the scenario the partnership lapses, it is perfectly possible and lawful for the three remaining entrepreneurs to continue in business with or without a written partnership agreement. This would constitute a new partnership.

ask: What advantages do sole proprietorship offer over other forms of business?

options.en: Greater control is vested in the hands of the sole proprietor and his liabilities are smaller
The personal liability of the sole proprietor makes lending to the proprietorship attractive
The sole proprietor faces a lower regulatory compliance burden, whether it is in the matter of disclosures or in the matter of accountability
The sole proprietor is able to bring his personal assets into the business
The sole proprietorship can own property if it is registered to do business outside the UK

explanation.en: Option C is correct. The sole proprietor faces a lower regulatory compliance burden, whether it is in the matter of disclosures or in the matter of accountability.

ask: What advantages does partnership offer over other forms of business?

options.en: Greater control is vested in the hands of the partners
The personal liability of the partners in most partnerships makes lending to the partnership attractive
The partners face a lower regulatory compliance burden, whether it is in the matter of disclosures or in the matter of accountability
The partnership starts with a smaller scope of business typically, and partners' liabilities are therefore within control
Depending on the terms of the partnership agreement and the size of a partnership, a partnership is more flexible in its operation than a company

explanation.en: Option E is the best answer. Depending on the terms of the partnership agreement and the size of a partnership, a partnership is more flexible in its operation than a company.

ask: Which of the following would you state as an advantage that cooperatives offer over other forms of business?

options.en: A cooperative provides greater flexibility than a partnership
A cooperative provides a greater say to its members than a company does to its shareholders
A cooperative can be formed for non-profit purposes only
Cooperatives are reputed to be more employee and community friendly
In the traditional form of a cooperative, members are part of one community with common aims. This in theory leads to focused, cohesive operations

explanation.en: Option E is correct. Often referred to as a "co-op," a cooperative is a limited liability entity that can organise for-profit or not-for-profit purposes. A cooperative differs from a corporation in that it has members, as opposed to shareholders, who share decision-making authority. Cooperatives are typically classified as either consumer cooperatives or worker cooperatives.

ask: What is the minimum number of directors required by the Companies Act to incorporate a private company?

explanation.en: Option B is correct. Private companies must have at least one director, and public companies at least two.

ask: Which of the following options best describes a company's ongoing regulatory burden?

options.en: The company must draw up detailed quarterly accounts
The company's accounts must be audited by an independent qualified accountant on a semi-annual basis and the audit reports filed with Companies House
The company is required to file a confirmation statement and pay a fee for filing it with Companies House
A private limited company must file disclosures about its entire staff earning more than £200,000 annually
A private limited company must hold board meetings each quarter

explanation.en: Option C is correct. A company is required to prepare a confirmation statement and to pay a fee on filing it with the Registrar of Companies. In that statement the company confirms that it has fulfilled all of its duties to notify the Registrar of Companies of any relevant changes. If the information held by Companies House is out of date the company must file the information needed to update its records before, or at the same time that it delivers the confirmation statement. The company and its officers may be liable criminally liable if a confirmation statement is not filed within 14 days of the end of the review period (which is a period of 12 months beginning (i) with the day of the company's incorporation or (ii) the day after the last review period, as appropriate). The confirmation statement must contain the company's name, number and the confirmation date. The filing must be signed or authenticated on behalf of the company. Note that option A in incorrect as the company's accounts must then be audited by an independent qualified accountant, necessitating an additional set of accountant's fees, annually (and not twice a year).

ask: Which option best describes what happens to profit earned by one partner from any use of the partnership property, name or business connection, without disclosing the circumstance to other partners?

options.en: The property is held on trust for the partnership, despite being owned by the partner

The property is held on trust for the partnership in perpetuity, unless the profiting partner discloses the circumstance to other partners and they consent to the profiting partner keeping the entirety or a share of the profits concerned
The property is held on trust for the partnership in perpetuity, unless the profiting partner discloses the circumstance to other partners, in which case the profiting partner automatically keeps it
The property is held on trust for the partnership in perpetuity, unless the partnership is determined, when it reverts to the partner who earned it
The property is held on trust for the partnership in perpetuity, unless there is a dispute between the partners, in which case, the matter is resolved legally

explanation.en: Option B is correct. All other options are incorrect. A trustee must not profit from his trust and this applies to partners as fiduciaries. Thus, a partner must not make unauthorised personal profit. Each partner must also account to the firm for any benefit derived without the consent of the other partners from any transaction concerning the partnership or from any use of the partnership's property, name or business connection. Any profit made in breach of s. 29 of the Partnership Act 1890 is thus held on trust for the partnership as a whole, unless the partners consent to the partner keeping the entirety or a share of the profits concerned, following full disclosure of the circumstances.

ask: Out of the five options of (i) limited liability, (ii) internal inflexibility, (iii) lack of privacy, (iv) complex setting up formalities, (v) legal uncertainty - what are the disadvantages that apply to an LLP?

options.en: (ii) internal inflexibility, (iii) lack of privacy, (iv) complex setting up formalities, (v) legal uncertainty
(iii) lack of privacy, (iv) complex setting up formalities, (v) legal uncertainty
(ii) internal inflexibility, (iii) lack of privacy, (iv) complex setting up formalities
(i) limited liability, (ii) internal inflexibility, (iii) lack of privacy
(i) limited liability, (ii) internal inflexibility, (iv) complex setting up formalities, (v) legal uncertainty

explanation.en: Option B is correct. All other options are incorrect. The advantages of an LLP include: limited liability (reduced risk to personal wealth from creditors' claims; and internal flexibility (which facilitates participation in management and maintenance of ethos of partnership), albeit that in the case of a small company the new Companies Act facilitates decision-making, for example by allowing meetings to be called on short notice, the use of written resolutions, and acceptance of informal unanimous assent). The disadvantages include: a lack of privacy (financial information must generally be disclosed); requirement for an LLP agreement (recommended to avoid default provisions applying and to cover situations not addressed by default provisions, unlike a company whose constitution acts as default standard provisions); legal uncertainty (novel structure - uncertainty is undesirable in commercial entities).

stem: Robert wishes to establish a business making replacement photocopier parts. He intends to employ Aaron and Bruce as workmen, who he will pay a salary, and Charles as a general manager who will carry out the day to day running of the business. Charles will be paid by being allocated a share of the profits of the business. Robert is funding the startup using a bank loan taken out in his own name.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Robert is a sole trader
Robert is in partnership with Charles
Robert is in partnership with Aaron, Bruce and Charles
Robert is a director of a limited company
Robert and Aaron are directors of a limited company

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Although Charles's salary is determined in accordance with the profits of the business, he is still an employee. He is not liable for the debts of the business and his employment can still be terminated by Robert. Robert is solely liable for the debts of the business and does not share this liability with anyone else.

stem: Anne, Bev and Carla wish to set up a business together. They intend that they will be jointly liable for the debts of the business and share equally in its profits. They have not filed any documentation at Companies House.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Anne, Bev and Carla are sole traders
Anne, Bev and Carla are in partnership
Anne, Bev and Carla are members of a limited liability partnership
Anne, Bev and Carla are members of a co-operative
Anne, Bev and Carla are directors of a limited company

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Anne, Bev and Carla intend that they will equally share the profits of the business as well as share equal liability for its debts. However as they have not created a separate legal personality for the business (by establishing a limited company or limited liability partnership) they are members of a partnership.

stem: Derek and Frank wish to go into business together. They both have a set amount of capital that they can invest into the business and do not wish their liability for the business' debts to exceed their investment.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Derek and Frank should set up a business as sole traders
Derek and Frank should set up a business as a partnership
Derek and Frank should set up a business as a limited liability partnership
Derek and Frank should set up a business as a limited company
Derek and Frank should set up a business as a limited liability partnership or as a limited company

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Both a limited liability partnership and limited company will afford Derek and Frank the protection of limited liability, meaning that they will not be liable for the debts of their business. Sole tradership is only suitable where one individual wishes to set up a business and a partnership will result in them being liable for all of the debts of the business.

stem: Donna and Ellen are partners. Their business has run up significant debts and its assets are not sufficient to meet its liabilities.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The creditors of the business are able to claim the debts from Donna and Ellen
The creditors of the business are able to claim the debts from Donna and Ellen and can issue proceedings for their bankruptcy if necessary
The creditors of the business can only claim up to the value of the business' assets
The creditors of the business can claim the debts from Donna and Ellen up to the value of their contributions to the business' capital
The creditors of the business are not able to claim the debts from Donna and Ellen

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Partners are jointly and severally liable for the debts of the business. All creditors of the business are able to claim for the debts of the business from the partners and have the partners' personal wealth and possessions available to them. If the partners' personal wealth is not sufficient to meet the liabilities of the business, then the creditors can issue proceedings for the bankruptcy of the partners if they wish to do so.

stem: Grace is preparing to set up an investment firm. She wishes to benefit from limited liability but is concerned that if she establishes a limited company, her home address will be available from Companies House as she will be a director of the company.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Grace will have to file her personal address at Companies House and should therefore opt to trade as a sole trader
Grace will have to file her personal address at Companies House and should therefore opt to trade in a limited liability partnership
Grace will have to file her personal address at Companies House but could still opt to trade as a limited company without having her personal address on the public record
Grace will not have to file her personal address at Companies House and should therefore opt to trade as a limited company
Grace will not have to file her personal address at Companies House and should therefore opt to trade as an unlimited company

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Every director must provide to Companies House both their usual residential address and a service address. The service address will be on the public record, whilst the residential address will be protected information. A director may choose to use his residential address as his service address. If this is the case, the service address will still appear on the public record, but the fact that the two addresses are the same will be protected information. Grace will therefore have to file her personal address at Companies House but could still opt to trade as a limited company without having her personal address on the public record.

stem: Harry and Jake wish to go into business together installing solar panels onto the roofs of residential property in England. They intend to be granted long leases of the airspace above the roofs by the residential owners which will give them the right to keep their solar panels there. Their long term business plan is to dispose of all of the leasehold interests to an investor who will collect the income generated by the panels. They are worried that transferring all of the individual leases to the investor may prove expensive. They also wish to benefit from limited liability.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: Harry and Jake should go into business as a partnership
Harry and Jake should go into business as a limited liability partnership
Harry and Jake should go into business as sole traders
Harry and Jake should form a limited company
Harry and Jake should form an unlimited company

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. If they establish their business as a limited company, then when they come to sell it they will simply have to transfer their shares to a purchaser rather than transfer all of the business' assets individually as they would have to do if they were established as a partnership or as sole traders. In order to benefit from unlimited liability, they would have to establish a limited rather than unlimited company.

stem: Robert and Aaron are in the process of establishing a limited company. They are asked by one of their investors to confirm the date upon which the company came into existence.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The company comes into existence when Robert and Aaron sign the Memorandum of Association
The company comes into existence when the first director is appointed
The company comes into existence when the documentation is filed at Companies House
The company comes into existence when a Certificate of Incorporation is issued
The company comes into existence on the start date specified in the application

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A limited company comes into existence when a Certificate of Incorporation is issued by Companies House on completion of the application.

stem: Anne, Bev and Carla form a limited company together and subscribe as the first members of the company. They each take 10,000 ordinary shares of £1.00 each in the company. Anne pays all of the shares up at the outset, Bev pays for £5,000 and Carla pays for none of them. The company is liquidated by its creditors and has debts exceeding £20,000.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The creditors can claim nothing from Anne Bev or Carla
The creditors can claim £20,000 from Anne, Bev and Carla jointly and severally
The creditors can claim £20,000 from Bev and Carla jointly and severally
The creditors can claim £5,000 from Bev and £10,000 from Carla
The creditors can claim £20,000 from Carla

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Members of a limited company have liability for the company's debts which is limited to the value of their unpaid shares. Anne is therefore not liable for any of the company's debts as all of her shares are paid up. Bev and Carla are therefore liable for the debts up to the value of their unpaid shares, £5,000 and £10,000 respectively.

stem: Bruce and Charles wish to start up a business to produce and market a new invention that they have come up with. They intend to raise capital by selling shares in their business to members of the public.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: They should establish a private limited company and will need at least £50,000 fully paid up share capital
They should establish a public limited company and will need at least £50,000 fully paid up share capital
They should establish a private limited company and will need at least £50,000 share capital, of which £12,500 must be fully paid up
They should establish a public limited company and will need at least £50,000 share capital, of which £12,500 must be fully paid up
They should establish a public limited company and will need at least £50,000 share capital, of which one quarter must be fully paid up

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. In order to sell shares in the company directly to the public, Bruce and Charles will have to establish a public limited company. A PLC needs to have a minimum share capital of £50,000 and one quarter of the share capital must be paid up at the time of incorporation. D is incorrect because £12,500 is not an absolute number, and will increase if the share capital is over £50,000.

stem: Two men are the members of Sample Limited; a third person is the company secretary; and two women are the directors of the company. A businessman is about to enter into a contract with Sample Limited and wishes to ensure that the correct person executes the contract.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The two men can execute the contract together
The company secretary can execute the contract only with either of the directors
Either of the directors can execute the contract
Either of the directors must execute the contract together with the company secretary
The contract can only be executed by the company secretary and the two directors together

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Either of the directors can execute the contract. Directors can act as agents of the company and are designated as such by the Companies Act 2006. They can usually act individually and there is no requirement for them to act jointly. The members of a company do not take any part in the day to day management of the company's affairs (unless they act in another capacity on behalf of the company).

stem: A man is the company secretary of Example Limited, a private company with two directors which carries on business as a car dealership. The man does not have any involvement in the day to day management of the business, which is usually left to the directors. The man receives a call from the dealership's manager who states that whilst the directors have been on an extended holiday, the majority of the stock has been sold, a pool car (for office use) has been destroyed in an accident and three of the staff have left. The man authorises the manager to place a further order for more stock vehicles, a new pool car and also to replace the staff. When the directors return, they state that they intend to close the business and try to cancel the orders and employment contracts the company secretary has entered into.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man can authorise the purchase of additional stock, the purchase of a new pool car and the employment of additional staff
The man can authorise the purchase of a new pool car and the employment of additional staff
The man can authorise the purchase of additional stock and the purchase of a new pool car
The man can authorise the purchase of additional stock and the employment of additional staff
The man can not authorise the purchase of additional stock, the purchase of a pool car or the employment of additional staff

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. A company secretary has ostensible authority to enter into contracts relating to a company's administrative affairs. They are not automatically authorised to enter into commercial contracts and would require specific authority to be delegated to them by the board in order to do so. Therefore in this scenario, the man only has authority to purchase a new pool car and hire additional staff, both actions which would be considered connected with the administrative operations of the company. They would not have the authority to purchase additional stock, which would be regarded as the entry into a commercial contract, an action reserved to directors.

stem: A woman is an executive director and Head of Legal Services for Example plc (Example). She is responsible for the sourcing of all legal services for Example. She is also a consultant and non-executive director of Full Circle Legal Limited (Full Circle), a private limited company carrying on business as a solicitors practice. Full Circle submits a tender in relation to a project which the woman wishes to outsource, but she awards the contract to another firm.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The woman has breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest that she owes to both Example and Full Circle
The woman has breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest that she owes to Example
The woman has breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest that she owes to Full Circle
The woman has not breached the duty to avoid conflicts of interest that she owes to neither Example nor Full Circle
The woman does not owe a duty to avoid conflicts of interest to either Example or Full Circle

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. As a director of both companies, whether an executive director or not, the woman owes each company a duty to avoid situations where her own interests may conflict with those of the company. Her duty to Example to obtain competitively priced legal services is therefore in conflict with her duty to Full Circle to maximise her income from fees. In order to avoid the situation from occurring, the woman should have resigned one of the directorships or else sought the approval of the other directors of both companies.

stem: A man is a director of Symbian Homes plc, a housebuilder company (Symbian). The man is also the owner of a large detached house in an area of countryside that Symbian has earmarked as a potential development zone. If the development goes ahead, the value of the man's home will reduce significantly. The man is concerned that his interests may soon be in conflict with those of Symbian.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man must resign as a director of Symbian
The man can continue to act as a director, but this must be approved by a special resolution of Symbian's members
The man can continue to act as a director, but this must be approved by an ordinary resolution of Symbian's members
The man can continue to act as a director, but this must be approved by a resolution of the other members of Symbian's board
The man can continue to act as a director provided that he is satisfied that no conflict of interest has in fact arisen

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A director is required to actively avoid situations in which he has - or could have had - any interest (direct or indirect) that conflicts (or may conflict) with the interests of the company. However the non-conflicted members of the board can authorise a conflicted director to continue to act provided that the requisite quorum exists, excluding the conflicted director.

stem: Example Limited is a private limited company and is a wholly owned subsidiary of International Holdings Limited. International Holdings Limited has designated its assistant company secretary, with responsibility of overseeing the operations of its subsidiaries and accordingly the assistant company secretary attends board meetings of Example, advising the directors what the wishes of the parent company may be in connection with any particular matter. The assistant company secretary has never been formally appointed as a director of Example Limited. Example Limited is now considering offering a takeover bid. The directors, knowing the parent company is, in fact, controlling Example Limited, act reluctantly in accordance with the assistant company secretary's advice who sets up the bid price and the terms of the bid.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The assistant company secretary owes no duties to Example Limited
The assistant company secretary would only owe limited duties to Example Limited
The assistant company secretary would owe the same duties to Example Limited as the directors of Example owe as he attends board meetings
The assistant company secretary would owe the same duties to Example Limited as the directors of Example owe because he is a shadow director
The assistant company secretary would owe the same duties to Example Limited as the directors of Example because he works for its holding company

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The assistant company secretary attends board meetings as a representative of Example Limited, International Holdings Limited's holding company, with a view to influencing the decisions made at board level. The board would be accustomed to acting in accordance with his instructions as he represents the members of the company. However, the assistant company secretary is not a member of the board. He would therefore be regarded as a shadow director for the purposes of the Companies Act 2006 and would owe the same duties to the company as an ordinary director.

stem: A man is an executive director of Example plc, a major UK energy supplier. He manages to persuade the board to advance him a loan of £200,000 in connection with an investment that he has been advised to make by his stockbroker. He guarantees the board that he will repay the loan within six months with 10% interest. At the end of the year, the company's accounts are put to the members and they query the loan.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The company has no power to make a loan to its directors
The loan to the man was lawful as it was made pursuant to a board resolution
The loan to the man should have been authorised by an ordinary resolution of the members
The loan to the man should have been authorised by a special resolution of the members
A company is free to make loans to whomever it wishes without the need for a board or members resolution

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Loans to directors that do not fit into the exceptions set out at sections 204 - 207 of the Companies Act 2006 are prohibited unless authorised by an ordinary resolution of the members of the company.

stem: A man is in the process of incorporating a company that he will use to run his family fishmongers business (which he previously operated as a sole trader), with the intention of protecting his personal assets from the business' creditors. He rebrands his business to reflect the change and continues to trade, without making any changes to the contracts he signed as a sole trader. The business fails and the company is liquidated, leaving substantial sums outstanding to the creditors.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man is not liable for any of the business debts as the company is a separate legal entity
The man is only liable for the business debts after the date that the company was incorporated
The man is only liable for the business debts which accrued prior to the date of incorporation
The man is only liable for the business debts where the contract giving rise to them was formed prior to the date of incorporation
The man is liable for all of the business debts as he is a member of the company

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. As the man was trading as a sole trader prior to the incorporation of the company, he will be liable for any debts where the contract giving rise to them was formed prior to the date of incorporation, even if the debts accrued after incorporation. Debts arising from contracts made after that date are the company's responsibility as it has a separate legal personality. As a member of the company, the man would only be liable to the creditors (via the liquidator) or the unpaid amount of his shares.

stem: Three men who are members of a private limited company been allotted 5,000 shares of £1 each. None of them have paid for the shares, although the articles require the members to pay for the shares when called upon to do so. The company runs into financial difficulty and is placed into liquidation by its creditors.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The three men are contractually liable to the company for all of its debts on a joint and several basis
The three men are contractually liable to the company for all of its debts
The three men are contractually liable to the company to pay £5,000 each
The three men are not liable to pay the company anything
The three men are contractually liable to the company's creditors for all of its debts

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The three men are liable under the company's articles to pay for the shares when called upon to do so. According to section 33 of the Companies Act 2006, the articles of association form a statutory contract between the members and the company and therefore the company can enforce the terms of the articles against the members as a contract. In this case, the articles provide that the members will be liable or their unpaid shares not the debts as a whole. As in all cases involving incorporated entities, the members are shielded from direct liability to the company's creditors because the limited company is deemed to have a separate legal personality and is therefore liable for its own debts.

stem: Example Limited is a prosperous property management company, owning rental properties all over the UK. The decision is taken to wind Example Limited up, as the directors and members no longer wish to continue trading. After the company's assets have been sold and its liabilities discharged, there is a significant amount of money left over.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The money will be distributed equally amongst the directors of the company
The money will be distributed equally amongst the members of the company
The money will be distributed amongst the members of the company according to their shareholdings
The money will be distributed amongst the directors of the company according to their remuneration agreements
The money will be held on trust for the company by the directors

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The company and all of its assets belong to the members, in proportions equate the placeballion Theteore when the companyi wound up andits shareholdings. The directors do not own the company or any of its assets (unless they are also members) and therefore they have no claim on the proceeds, other than as creditors of the company if they are owed anything.

stem: A man holds 20% of the shareholding in Example Limited, a small private company. A woman holds the other 80% of the shareholding and is also the sole director of the company. Although the articles provide that the directors shall declare dividends where the company's operating profit exceeds a certain amount, the woman consistently refuses to do so and instead pays herself large fees to keep the company's profits below the level where a dividend could be paid.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The man could bring a derivative claim against the woman under the common law rules
The man could bring a derivative claim against the woman under the Companies Act
The man could bring a derivative claim against the woman under either the Companies Act 2006 or the common law rules
The man could enforce the terms of the articles against the woman in contract
The man could bring an action under section 994 of the Companies Act 2006 for unfair prejudice

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A derivative claim is brought by a shareholder in the name of the company where a director has caused loss to the company by reason of a breach of duty to the company. The common law rules have now been replaced by the statutory scheme under the Companies Act 2006 and are therefore obsolete and could not be used. The terms of the articles are treated as a contract between the members of the company however the woman is acting in her capacity as a director in refusing to pay dividends. The correct means of redress would be for the man to bring an action under section 994 of the Companies Act 2006 on the basis that he is being unfairly prejudiced.

stem: Three men are members of Example Limited, a private company. The first man holds 20% of the voting shares, the second holds 20% and the third 60%. A fourth person is the sole director of the company. At the annual members meeting, a resolution is tabled to remove a fourth director eight months before the end of his term of office.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The resolution could be passed if the first man was in favour but the second and third opposed it
The resolution could be passed if the second man was in favour but the first and third men opposed it
The resolution could be passed if the third man was in favour but the first and second men opposed it
The resolution could be passed if the first and second men were in favour but the third man opposed it
The resolution could only be passed if the members were unanimous

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The removal of a director from office by the members is achieved by an ordinary resolution, carrying a simple majority of over 50% of the votes. This is prescribed in the Companies Act 2006 and therefore the articles of the company cannot prescribe a higher majority to be required. As the first and second men between them only hold 40% of the voting shares, the third man must consent to the resolution in order for it to be passed.

stem: Three partners carry on business together as dentists. One partner is notified by her regulator that a complaint has been made against her by a member of the public. She is confident that the complaint will not succeed and therefore does not tell her partners about this when the firm is bidding for a lucrative contract providing services to a third party. The firm wins the contract but when the complaint against the partner succeeds and she is prevented from practising, the firm is unable to meet its obligations under the contract. The third party sues the firm for damages.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: All of the partners are jointly and severally liable to the third party for loss arising from the breach of contract
The partner unable to practise is solely liable to the third party for loss arising from the breach of contract
The remaining two partners are jointly and severally liable to the third party for loss arising from the breach of contract

All of the partners are jointly and severally liable to the third party for loss arising from the breach of contract but the partner unable to practise is liable to indemnify the remaining two partners
Only the partner unable to practise is liable to the third party for loss arising from the breach of contract but is liable to be indemnified by the remaining two partners

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. As the partnership continues in existence notwithstanding the failure of the defaulting partner to notify her partners of her inability to practise, all of the partners are able to bind each other as agents and they are therefore jointly and severally liable to third parties.
