However as a partnership is a contract of the utmost good faith, each partner must deal openly and honestly with the others and is under a positive obligation to disclose facts affecting the business to the other partners. A failure to discharge this duty would render her liable to account to the other partners for any loss that they suffer as a result.

stem: Two partners carry on business as solicitors. One partner is looking to raise a loan to meet the costs of his divorce and charges his share in the partnership to the lender as security. He defaults on the loan and the lender enforces its security.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The lender is able to become involved in the management of the partnership business, to require production of partnership accounts and records, to monitor financial transactions and to collect the profits generated by the share in the business charged to the lender
The lender is able to require production of partnership accounts and records, to monitor financial transactions and to collect the profits generated by the share in the business charged to the lender
The lender is able to monitor financial transactions and to collect the profits generated by the share in the business charged to the lender
The lender is able to collect the profits generated by the share in the business charged to the lender

The lender is not able to become involved in the management of the partnership business, to require production of partnership accounts and records, to monitor financial transactions and to collect the profits generated by the share in the business charged to the lender

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. An assignee of a share in a partnership business is not entitled to intermeddle in the affairs of the partnership or to require the partners to account for any specific transactions or even to produce accounts. An assignee is simply entitled to receive the profits accruing to the assigned share and to receive a proportion of the partnership assets on dissolution of the partnership.

stem: Three partners set up a business together as a solicitors practice. There is no partnership deed. The practise is extremely successful and the partners become very wealthy. One partner sets up his own side business as a property developer, which he operates at weekends. Gradually the property development business begins to take over more and more of his time and the other partners become concerned that this is affecting the partnership.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The partner is in competition with the firm. He will be liable to pay over profits to the partnership and the court could make an injunction preventing him from carrying on the business
The partner is in competition with the firm. He will be liable to pay over profits to the partnership
The partner is in competition with the firm. The court could make an injunction preventing him from carrying on the business
The partner is not in competition with the firm and the other partners have no remedy against him
There are no restrictions on a partner being in competition with their firm

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Section 30 Partnership Act 1890 provides that a partner must not engage in a business which is in competition with that carried on by the firm. However there is no statutory restriction on engaging in other business activities provided that they do not compete with the business of the firm and any such restriction would have to be included in a partnership deed.

stem: Three persons wish to go into business together. They are attracted to the flexibility of the partnership model but wish to limit their liability and decide to form a limited liability partnership. They do not enter into a membership agreement but make the necessary application at Companies House to register the LLP.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The LLP is formed when the partners go into business together
The LLP is formed when the partners sign a membership agreement
The LLP is formed when the application to Companies House is signed
The LLP is formed when Companies House issues a certificate of incorporation
The LLP is formed on the making of a court order to that effect

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. An LLP is a corporate entity with a separate legal personality. Unlike a general partnership, which is formed by the relationship of the members going into business with each other (and if formed de facto), an LLP is a statutory association that is formed de juris on the completion of certain legal formalities, culminating in the issue of a certificate of incorporation.

stem: A group of friends plan to start a business. They want to ensure their liability is limited but also want each person to have equal decision- making authority.
ask: Which of the following business models would be most appropriate for group?

options.en: Fixed term partnership
Sole Proprietorship
Corporation
Cooperative
Partnership at will

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A Co-op allows the group to limit their liability and also allows members to have equal decision- making authority.

stem: A man has been offered the position of non-executive director. He is unsure exactly what the role of a non-executive director is.
ask: Advise the man regarding the nature of the role?

options.en: A non- executive director has the same responsibilities as a director
A non-executive director is responsible for the day to day running of the business
A non-executive director is involved with the planning and policy making but not in the day to day running of the business
A non- executive director is involved with the planning and policy making and in the day to day running of the business
The term 'non-executive director' is interchangeable with 'company secretary'

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. A non-executive director is often appointed because of their knowledge of their industry, their business prowess, their experience etc. They are involved in the planning and policy making but not the day to day running of the business.

stem: m A man is in the process of setting up a private limited company but is not sure who will remain personally liable for the debts of the business.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains the situation?

options.en: Only the person or persons who form the corporation remain personally liable
The directors remain personally liable but only during their time on the board
No one is personally liable for the debts of the business, unless it is a one-member company with only one director
No one is personally liable for the debts of the business, unless it is a one-member company
No one is personally liable for the debts of the business

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A limited company is a separate legal entity and therefore its shareholders have no personal liability in relation to the debts of the business.

stem: A man wants to set up a business alone but does not want to be personally liable for the debts of the business.
ask: What type of business model would allow the man to limit his liability?

options.en: Sole proprietorship
Corporation
Partnership at will
Fixed term partnership
Cooperative

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. A sole proprietorship would not allow them man to limit his liability and a partnership or cooperative wouldn't be appropriate as the man wants to own the business without partners or members. Therefore, the option most suited to the man is a corporation as this will allow his to avoid personal liability for the debts belonging to the business.

stem: Three people decide to form a partnership. They want to know whether there is any way to limit their liability whilst remaining a partnership.
ask: Advise them of the relevant legal position?

options.en: A partnership can never offer limited liability
A partnership always offers limited liability
A limited liability partnership limits liability of all partners
A limited liability partnership limits liability of some partners
A standard partnership limits liability if there are over three partners

explanation.en: The best answer is C. A limited liability partnership will limit the liability of all the partners, also known as 'members'.

stem: Your client has worked on a self-employed basis for the past two years. She is now being held personally liable for debts owed by the business. She believes she is not personally liable as the business is separate entity. She is not registered with Companies House and works alone.
ask: Which of the following best describes your client's situation?

options.en: Your client is a director of a business and is not, therefore, personally liable
Your client is a shareholder of a corporation and is not, therefore, personally liable
Your client is a sole trader but does not have personal liability
Your client is a sole trader and does have personal liability
Your client is a sole trader and does have limited personal liability

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Your client has not fulfilled the requirements of setting up a corporation or partnership. She is, therefore, a sole trader, and as a sole trader, she is personally liable for debts incurred by the business.

stem: A woman is considering an offer of becoming a director in a company. Before accepting the offer, she would like to know
ask: What the sanctions are if she breaches her duties as a director. Advise the woman?

options.en: A breach of a duty results in civil sanctions only
A breach of a duty results in criminal sanctions only
A breach of a duty results in loss of directorship only
A breach of a duty can result in civil sanctions and loss of directorship
A breach of a duty can result in civil and/or criminal sanctions and/or loss of directorship

explanation.en: The best answer is E. Depending on the nature of the breach and actions of the directors, a breach of duty can result in criminal and/or civil sanctions and/or loss of directorship.

stem: A man wishes to sue an unlimited company for invoices that have not been paid. The company cannot meet its financial obligations to its creditors and goes into liquidation. Believing that the members are personally liable, he sues two women who are members of the company. The women claim the man cannot sue them personally for the debt.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Members of an unlimited company are not personally liable for the debts of the business during its normal course of business and in liquidation
Members of an unlimited company can be sued directly for the debts of the business in liquidation
Members of an unlimited company can be liable for the debts of the business, if the claim is made in liquidation rather than suing the members directly
No claim can be made against the members of an unlimited company, unless otherwise decided by the liquidator
A claim against the members directly must be made within six months of the debt occurring

explanation.en: The best answer is C. Members of an unlimited company can be liable for the debts of the business, if the claim is made in liquidation rather than suing the members directly. An unlimited company is a legal entity where the legal liability of the members is not limited, i.e., its members have a joint, several and non-limited obligation to meet any insufficiency in the assets of the company to enable settlement of any outstanding financial liability in the event of the company's formal liquidation. Therefore, prior to any such formal liquidation of the unlimited company, any creditors or security holders of the company may only have recourse to the assets of the company and not to those of its members. Until formal liquidation occurs, an unlimited company is similar to the limited company where its members have no direct liability to the creditors or security holders during its normal course of business or existence. The creditors cannot sue the members directly, but must claim in the liquidation, from the liquidator, who then calls for contributions from the members.

stem: David owns and operates a business called "David's Tools", which employs three workers to staff a shop. David has taken out a loan in his own name to fund the start-up, and any profits that the business makes belong to David.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: David's Tools is a limited company
David's Tools is an LLP
David's Tools is a partnership
David's Tools is a co-operative
David's Tools is run by David as a sole trader

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. David's Tools is run by David as a sole trader. This is evidenced by the fact that David is himself liable for the business' debts, and that he is likewise entitled to all of its profits.

stem: Three solicitors agree to set themselves up to practise together. All of their fees are paid into a shared office account out of which they pay costs of running their shared office premises and support staff and take their own salaries. Although they have never expressly decided to set up a partnership and there is no written partnership agreement, they meet regularly to discuss various issues of management of the office and their brand in general.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the position?

options.en: The operation is a partnership
The operation is not a partnership, because it does not carry on a business
The operation is not a partnership, because the solicitors are not carrying on business in common
The operation is not a partnership, because the solicitors are not carrying on business with a view to profit
The operation is not a partnership, because the solicitors have not entered into a partnership agreement

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The requirements of a partnership contained in s.1 of the Partnership Act 1890 have been satisfied. There is no requirement that a written partnership agreement is in place and no registration requirements and therefore a partnership will exist if the requirements contained in the Act are satisfied.

stem: Three people wish to go into business together and to ensure that whichever business structure they use allows them the flexibility to make decisions regarding all aspects of the business based upon a simple 2 to 1 majority. The capital for the business is to be provided by loans which the business partners themselves will provide. They wish the formation and operation of the business to be as fast as possible with minimal formality and the affairs of the business to remain secret.
ask: Which option offers the best advice to the three people?

options.en: They would be best advised to set up a limited company
They would be best advised to set up a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)
They would be best advised to form a partnership
They would be best advised to form a co-operative
They would be best advised to establish themselves as sole traders

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. They should form a partnership. A partnership allows for a high degree of flexibility regarding decision making and, since no filings are required, the affairs of the business, such as its finances and membership, can remain secret. A partnership is relatively easy to establish, meaning that the set up costs are minimal. The opposite is true of a limited company, where there is a high initial set up cost as well as many on-going responsibilities in terms of disclosure of the company's affairs and general administration.

stem: Two men are deciding on a name for their company. As a partnership, the first partner thinks they are still required to register the name with Companies House but the other partner believes there are no restrictions when naming a partnership.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: There are no restrictions when naming a partnership
The name of the company must be registered at Companies House
The name must not violate the Business Names Act 1985 and must be registered at Companies House
The name must be approved by the courts, adhere to the Business Names Act 1985 and be registered at Companies House
The name must not violate the Business Names Act 1985

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The name of a partnership does not need to be registered or approved but is must comply with the Business Names Act 1985.

stem: A man has been working as a self-employed for the past eight months. He works alone and does not employ anyone or use subcontractors. The business is not a separate legal entity and the man remains personally liable for any debts the business has.
ask: Which type of business does the man have?

options.en: Partnership at will
Corporation
Sole proprietorship (sole trader)
Public Limited Company
Fixed term partnership

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The details of the man's business and his personally liability indicate the he is a sole trader. He has no partners which rules out the business being a partnership and the fact that the business is not a separate legal entity means it cannot be a corporation or PLC.

stem: You act for the directors of a private company limited by shares, with no objects and model articles of association. The directors authorised by resolution a sales agent to enter into contracts on behalf of the company up to a value of £500,000. The sales agent contracted with another company that is 30% owned by one of the directors of the company for a contract worth £650,000. The shareholders of your clients' company are deeply unhappy with this turn of events and are threatening action. The directors want to know their options to protect the contract.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The contract is still enforceable, but voidable at the instance of the company, unless the transaction is affirmed or the company is indemnified against any loss or damage resulting from the transaction
The agent acted ultra vires and the contract is automatically voided. No recourse is available to the directors
The contract is still enforceable, because the contracting company acted in good faith and had no reason to know, suspect or enquire as to any limitations on the agent's ability to contract with them

The contract is still enforceable, but voidable at the instance of the company, because the contracting company did not enquire with the agent as to any limitations on his authority. The directors must personally indemnify the company against any loss or damage arising from the transaction
The contract is still enforceable, because the doctrine of ultra vires no longer exists

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The contract is still enforceable, but voidable at the instance of the company, unless the transaction is affirmed or the company is indemnified against any loss or damage resulting from the transaction. Under section 41(2) of the Companies Act 2006 (the Act), where a company enters into a transaction and the parties include a director of the company, its holding company, or a person connected with any such director, the transaction is voidable at the instance of the company. Under section 254, a director is connected with a body corporate when they have an interest in at least 20% of the share capital or exercise more than 20% of the voting power of that company. In this case, the company with which the agent transacted, 30% owned by a director of the company, that will be considered a body corporate 'connected with' a director of the company, thus falling under the provisions of section 41 of the Act. Therefore, the transaction is voidable at the instance of the company, unless one or more of the four conditions of section 41(4) are met. These are: the restitution of any money or other asset which was the subject matter of the transaction is no longer possible, or the company is indemnified for any loss or damage resulting from the transaction, or rights acquired bona fide for value and without actual notice of the directors' exceeding their powers by a person who is not party to the transaction would be affected by the avoidance, or the transaction is affirmed by the company.

stem: The articles of association of a private company limited by shares states that the company's business is the production of footwear in the UK. Due to the economic downturn, the company contracts with China for more cost-efficient production of one of the company's products. A minority shareholder is aggrieved at this but the majority shareholders understand the decision and are happy with it. They approach you for advice on how to protect the company's position.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The shareholders cannot act to protect the position - the directors must do so
The shareholders can ratify the actions of the directors
The shareholders must sue the directors in the company name for an indemnity for any loss or damage arising from the transaction
The shareholders must sue the directors in their individual names for an indemnity for any loss or damage arising from the transaction
The shareholders must pass a special resolution to alter the articles of association to justify the transaction

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Under section 239 of the Companies Act 2006 (the Act), the members can ratify the conduct of a director or directors amounting to negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust in relation to the company. In this case there is an arguable breach of the directors of their duty to act within the company's constitution under section 171 of the Act. The ratification must be made by members' resolution. It is passed either by written resolution where neither the director(s) concerned nor any connected member is eligible to vote, or at a meeting where the necessary majority is only obtained disregarding votes in favour of the resolution by the director(s) and any member connected with them. The director(s) or connected member can still attend, make quorum and take part in other business.

stem: You are approached by the directors of a private company limited by shares, formed just under a year ago. The company has performed well and the shareholders want to know whether a dividend will be paid this year.
ask: What are the statutory requirements that must be met in order for a company to pay a dividend to shareholders?

options.en: A company may pay a dividend out of any funds it has available
A company may pay a dividend only out of original capital
A company may pay a dividend only out of available profits
A company must pay a dividend and only out of available profits
A company may pay a dividend only from revenue

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. A company may pay a dividend only out of available profits. Section 830(1) of the Companies Act 2006 states that a company may only make a distribution out of profits available for the purpose. Section 830(2) defines available profits as a company's "accumulated, realised profits, so far as not previously utilised by distribution or capitalisation, less its accumulated, realised losses, so far as not previously written off in a reduction or reorganisation of capital duly made."

stem: You are advising directors of a private limited company formed less than one year ago. The shareholders took a big risk investing in the company, which has yielded stunning results in a very short time. The directors wish to repay the risk of the shareholders by paying out a dividend before the company's first anniversary of inception. However, the first set of annual accounts has not yet been circulated.
ask: Which of the following best advises the directors of their available options?

options.en: The directors cannot make a dividend payment until the first set of annual accounts have been approved and filed with the registrar
The directors can make a dividend payment before the first set of annual accounts, but must use interim accounts that show the company to meet the statutory requirements in order to pay a dividend

The directors can make a dividend payment before the first set of annual accounts, but must make a statutory declaration that they consider the company to possess the requisite available profits to pay the dividend

The directors can make a dividend payment before the first set of annual accounts, but must use initial accounts that enable a reasonable judgement to be made as to the amounts of the profits, losses, assets, liabilities, share capital and reserves

The directors can make a dividend payment before the first set of accounts, but must use initial accounts that enable a reasonable judgement to be made that the company is on track to suitable profitability to enable the payment to be made

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The directors can make a dividend payment before the first set of annual accounts, but must use initial accounts that enable a reasonable judgement to be made as to the amounts of the profits, losses, assets, liabilities, share capital and reserves. Section 836 of the Companies Act 2006 provides the basis on which a distribution may be justified - by reference to the company's accounts. Section 836(1) requires that the profits, losses, assets, liabilities, provisions based on whether the accounts are Companies Act or IAS accounts and share capital and reserves (including undistributable reserves) are stated in the accounts and referred to. Under section 836(2) the relevant accounts are the company's last accounts, except where, as in this case, the distribution is proposed to be declared during the company's first accounting reference period, or before any accounts have been circulated in respect of that period, in which case initial accounts may be used. Under section 839(1), the initial accounts must enable a reasonable judgment to be made as to the amounts of the items listed in section 836(1) (profit, loss etc.)

stem: A private company limited by shares has two executive directors who are not members, and four shareholders each having 25% of the issued capital of the company. The company normally pays an annual dividend to its members, but have decided not to this year. However, the directors award themselves bonuses worth 25% of their salary, and refuse to lay the accounts before the members so as to conceal this decision. The members find out and are incensed and bring an 'unfair prejudice' application before the court. The company has model articles of association.
ask: Which of the following best describes what remedy, if any, the members can seek?

options.en: The court is not permitted to interfere in the management of a private company. No remedy is permissible
The court must disqualify the directors
The court must nullify the directors' decision
The court can only allow civil proceedings to be brought in the name of the company by the aggrieved members
The court may order any remedy it thinks fit

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The court may order any remedy it thinks fit. The powers of the court in respect of an 'unfair prejudice' brought under section 994 (or section 995 if brought on behalf of the Secretary of State) of the Companies Act 2006 ('the Act') is contained in section 996(1), which affords, where a court is satisfied that a petition is well-founded, to make such order as it thinks fit for giving relief in respect of the matters complained of. This is a very wide discretion, and is supplemented (but not governed) by the provisions of section 996(2), all of which are options for orders that the court may make. All answers apart from E are therefore wrong, because the court is not mandated to implement any specific remedy. Whilst the test for 'unfair prejudice' is objective, the appropriate remedy turns on the facts of each case and is for the court to decide.

stem: You act for a man with a 20% shareholding in a private company limited by shares, which has five members in total. At a meeting attended by four of the shareholders - who live close to each other - in a remote location that was too far away and at too short notice for the fifth 'troublemaking' member, a special resolution was passed altering the company's articles of association to remove the voting rights of the shares held by this fifth member. Your client has since aligned himself with the concerns of this 'troublemaking shareholder' and wishes to take action to remedy this situation.
ask: Which of the following best advises your client?

options.en: Your client can bring a petition to court on the grounds that the company's affairs have been conducted in a way that is grossly prejudicial to the 'troublemaking shareholder's' interests. The test is subjective

Your client can bring a petition to court on the grounds that the company's affairs have been conducted in a way that is grossly prejudicial to the 'troublemaking shareholder's' interests. The test is objective

Your client can bring a petition to court on the grounds that the company's affairs have been conducted in a way that is unfairly prejudicial to the 'troublemaking shareholder's' interests. The test is objective

Your client can bring a petition to court on the grounds that the company's affairs have been conducted in a way that is unfairly prejudicial to the 'troublemaking shareholder's' interests. The test is subjective
Your client cannot bring a petition to the court in respect of the 'troublemaking shareholder'

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Your client cannot bring a petition to the court in respect of the 'troublemaking shareholder'. Under section 994 of the Companies Act 2006, a member may bring a petition to court for an order remedying the situation on the grounds that that the past, current or proposed actions have or will be unfairly prejudicial to the interests of the members generally, or part of those members. However, this section specifically states that the petitioner themselves must be unfairly prejudiced by that which is the subject of the petition. In this case, your client was not unfairly prejudiced, and therefore has no locus standi to bring the action. The 'troublemaking shareholder' would have to bring his own petition. Had your client also been unfairly prejudiced, he could bring the petition to include himself and the 'troublemaking shareholder'.

stem: Two women and a man run a business as a partnership. They have a formal partnership agreement in place which includes a simply-worded expulsion clause, allowing them to expel a partner in the event of that partner's bankruptcy. The male partner is declared bankrupt after his personal life goes off the rails. The two women wish to expel the partner and continue the partnership, which is very profitable. The male partner insists that the expulsion clause isn't valid and that the partnership must automatically dissolve.
ask: Which of the following correctly describes the legal position?

options.en: An expulsion clause has no practical legal effect: the partnership is automatically dissolved on the bankruptcy of a partner and the assets must be sold
An expulsion clause is valid only with the unanimous consent of all partners, which is not the case here
The expulsion clause is valid: the male partner is expelled from the partnership, the partnership continues to exist and the remaining partners must buy the expelled partner's share of the assets
The expulsion clause is valid: the male partner is expelled but his share of the partnership assets form part of his estate in bankruptcy
The expulsion clause is valid: the male partner is expelled and his share of the partnership assets automatically transfers to the remaining partners

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The expulsion clause is valid: the male partner is expelled from the partnership, the partnership continues to exist and the remaining partners must buy the expelled partner's share of the assets. Under section 25 of the Partnership Act 1890 (the 'Act'), no majority of the partners can expel any partner unless a power to do so has been conferred by express agreement between the partners." Since express provision has been made by way of expulsion clause in the partnership agreement, the female partners can legally expel the male partner and allow the partnership to continue. In the absence of such a provision, the partner's bankruptcy would have automatically dissolved the partnership under section 33 of the Act.

stem: A firm of three partners approaches you for advice. Their partnership has run into difficult financial times, compounded by the death of one of their fellow founding partners. Despite an express provision allowing the partnership to continue in the death of a partner and the partnership remaining solvent, they have decided to wind up the partnership and are unsure of the process to follow, as they have never had any partnership agreement in place.
ask: Which of the following best represents the legal position and course of events that follows?

options.en: The partners may voluntarily dissolve the partnership, but on doing so will cease to have any authority to bind the partnership, and must appoint a receiver to value and sell the assets of the partnership and pay off any debts

The partners can only dissolve the partnership on application to the court for an order dissolving the partnership and appointing a receiver, who will value and sell the partnership assets and pay off any debts

The partners must enter into a voluntary and binding agreement with creditors, and must then value the partnership assets, which will be sold in accordance with fulfilling the requirements of the voluntary agreement

The partners may voluntarily dissolve the partnership and will retain such continuing authority as is necessary to finish transactions and wind up the partnership. The partners must value and sell the partnership assets and pay off any outstanding debts
The partners may voluntarily dissolve the partnership and personally keep their respective shares of the assets

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The partners may voluntarily dissolve the partnership and will retain such continuing authority as is necessary to finish transactions and wind up the partnership. The partners must value and sell the partnership assets and pay off any outstanding debts.

stem: You work in the corporate department of a multi-disciplined law firm. Your colleague in the litigation department is commencing proceedings against a private company limited by shares. He serves the documents on the company secretary at the company's registered office. In the covering letter with the Acknowledgment of Service, the director of the company points out that the company does not have a secretary. Your colleague believes that the company is neither a valid entity nor that proceedings have been validly served.
ask: Which of the following is the best advice you can give your colleague?

options.en: A private company is not required to have a secretary, and the proceedings will be considered validly served, as, where a company has no secretary, anything addressed to the secretary is considered as addressed to the company
A private company is required to have a secretary and is not considered validly incorporated without one

A private company is not required to have a secretary, but documents sent to a company without a secretary must be addressed to the company itself and not its secretary, otherwise they will not be validly served
A private company is required to have a secretary. Until this is remedied, documents must be sent to the company itself in order to be considered validly served
A private company is not required to have a secretary, and any documents served on a company must name a director in order to be validly served

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. A private company is not required to have a secretary, and the proceedings will be considered validly served, as, where a company has no secretary, anything addressed to the secretary is considered as addressed to the company. Under section 270(1) of the Companies Act 2006 (the 'Act'), a private company is not required to have a secretary. Under section 270(2) of the Act, where a private company has no secretary, anything required to be served on the company by being given to the secretary may be served on the company itself, and if addressed to the secretary shall be treated as addressed to the company. The documents were, therefore, validly served.

stem: You act for one of the directors of a private company. They are in the process of converting into a public company and are dealing with the appointment of a secretary. They are unsure as to the qualifications required of the secretary, and present you with a shortlist of possible candidates.
ask: Which of the following is eligible to be appointed the company secretary?

options.en: The director is misguided: there are no qualification requirements for the secretary of a public company
A person formerly a secretary of another public company for two of the past five years
A trainee solicitor
A non-chartered self-employed bookkeeper who has never held any other positions
A person with no formal qualifications but extensive business experience and who has held several secretarial positions at private limited companies in the past

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A person with no formal qualifications but extensive business experience and who has held several secretarial positions at private limited companies in the past is eligible to be appointed as secretary of a public company. Section 271 of the Companies Act 2006 (the 'Act') requires a public company to have a secretary. Section 273 of the Act requires that the directors of a public company take all reasonable steps to secure that the secretary has the requisite knowledge and experience to discharge the functions of company secretary and has suitable qualifications (so Answer A is wrong). Those qualifications are: (a) that he has held the office of secretary of a public company for at least three of the five years immediately preceding his appointment as secretary (so B is wrong); (b) that he is a member of any of the bodies specified in subsection (3) - these are chartered institutions; (c) that he is a barrister, advocate or solicitor called or admitted in any part of the United Kingdom (so C is wrong as a trainee is not yet qualified); or (d) that he is a person who, by virtue of his holding or having held any other position or his being a member of any other body, appears to the directors to be capable of discharging the functions of secretary of the company. Based on the above qualifications, the non-chartered bookkeeper has neither the formal qualifications nor do they likely have the experience of holding other positions to fulfil the qualification requirements. The person with extensive business experience who has previously held positions would be the only candidate who meets the qualification requirements.

stem: You are advising the directors of a small private limited company on filing and administrative requirements. They have appointed a secretary but are unsure of the record- keeping requirements.
ask: Which of the following explains the record-keeping requirements of companies in respect of secretaries?

options.en: Only Companies House (the registrar) must be notified of appointments and resignations of secretaries. There are no other record-keeping requirements

A company must keep a register of secretaries in addition to notifying the registrar of any changes, but the register does not need to be made available for inspection. Failing to comply with these requirements is a criminal offence

A company must keep a register of secretaries in addition to notifying the registrar of any changes. The register must be made available for inspection. Failing to comply with these requirements can result in a civil sanction

A company must keep a register of secretaries in addition to notifying the registrar of any changes. The register must be made available for inspection. Failing to comply with these requirements is a criminal offence

A company must keep a register of secretaries in addition to notifying the registrar of any changes. The register must be made available for inspection. The name of the secretary must also be displayed on all letterheads and company stationery. Failing to comply with these requirements is a civil offence

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. In addition to the duty to notify the registrar of any changes in respect of company secretaries (section 276 Companies Act 2006), a company must keep a register of its secretaries under section 275(1). It must contain the required particulars (section 275(2)) and be available for inspection at the company's registered office or any other specified place (section 275(3)). Any changes in the location of the register must be notified to the registrar (section 275(4)). Failure to comply with these provisions is a criminal offence (section 275(6)). There is no requirement for secretary details to be displayed on any stationery.

stem: Two business men want to start a company. One of them believes that any limited company can sell shares to the public, whilst his friend argues that only public limited companies can do so.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Only public limited companies can sell shares to the public
Private or public limited companies can sell shares to the public
Private and public limited companies, as well as unlimited companies, can sell shares to the public
Any type of business can sell shares to general public if they comply with securities laws
Public limited companies can sell shares to the public if they were previously private for at least 12 months

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Only public limited companies can sell shares to the public.

stem: The share capital of SeriousDrinks Ltd is owned by five different shareholders: (i) David holds 31% of the shares; (ii) Jim holds 26% of the shares; (iii) the Jane Vardy Trust, a trust registered in a jurisdiction in which it does not have legal personality, holds 23% of the shares, as nominee for Jane Vardy's son James who is the beneficial owner and who directs the trust's activities;(iv) Sean holds 14% of the shares; and (v) Robert holds the final 6% of the shares. Sean and Robert are also directors of SeriousDrinks Ltd and the other owners generally follow Robert's advice when voting on resolutions at general meetings. Each share in SeriousDrinks Ltd carries one vote at meetings. The directors of SeriousDrinks Ltd have read that they need to prepare a register of persons with significant control.
ask: Which persons should be included in the PSC Register?

options.en: David, Jim, and Robert
David, Jim, the trustees of the Jane Vardy Trust, and Robert
David, Jim, James, Sean and Robert
David, Jim and James Vardy
David, Jim, the trustees of the Jane Vardy Trust, James Vardy and Robert

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Every company must maintain a register of individuals and legal entities with significant control over the company (known as the "PSC Register"). David owns more than 25% of the shares in SeriousDrinks Ltd and therefore must be included in the PSC Register. Jim also qualifies due to his 26% stake. Neither the trustees of the Jane Vardy Trust nor James Vardy need to be included as the holding is less than 25% and they do not qualify under any of the other grounds. Sean fails to qualify with his 14% stake, even though he is also a director. However, although Robert's stake is only 6%, he has influence over voting patterns at general meetings. For this reason, he must be included in the PSC Register, as a person is also classified as having significant control, even if he owns 25% or less of the shares or voting rights in the company, if he is actually exercising significant control or influence over the company, which seems to be the case in the fact pattern.

stem: A group of scientists have produced a beauty serum from a peculiar source. The amount invested by each scientist differs significantly. Lab results suggest that the product easily outperforms its competitors in the market. The product is ready to sell; however, the scientists are unsure how well it will be received in the market given it is so unusual. To expedite entry to market, the scientists intend to commence trading without incorporating any form of business entity.
ask: Advise the scientists which of the following statements best reflects the position?

options.en: Irrespective of any difference in the amounts invested, each scientist will be fully liable for the obligations of the business of the group
Any business debt incurred during trading must be satisfied from the sale of assets held by the group
The creditors of each individual may obtain payment from the group as a whole or in such proportion as the creditor may determine
Should any contractual or tortious liability be incurred by the group, the scientists will be jointly and severally liable for the resulting obligation
Each scientist will be liable to contribute to the debts of the group in such proportion as his capital investment

explanation.en: The best answer is A. Irrespective of any difference in the amounts invested, each scientist will be fully liable for the obligations of the business of the group. A partnership will exist if the definition provided by section 1(1) of the Partnership Act 1890 is satisfied; namely, "partnership is the relation which subsists between persons carrying on business in common with a view of profit". An entity incorporated pursuant to the Companies Act 2006 or any other legislation, such as the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2000, is not a partnership as provided by section 1(2) of the 1890 Act. The scientists will, therefore, be bound in partnership if the business is not transferred into an incorporated entity. Section 9 of the 1890 Act provides that every partner is liable jointly with the other partners for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while he is a partner. It follows that irrespective of any difference in the amounts invested, each scientist will be fully liable for the obligations of the business of the partnership. It should be noted that it is not accurate to state that the scientists will be jointly and severally liable for any contractual or tortious liability incurred by the group as the liability of partners is only joint and several in the case of tortious obligations; it is joint in respect of contractual obligations.

stem: A director of a company, who is also a shareholder of XYZ Limited, wishes to purchase his company car from XYZ Limited. The company has adopted the Model Articles (unamended). The director has made a declaration of his interest in the proposed purchase of the car.
ask: Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.en: The director could only be prevented from participating in the decision making process for quorum purposes at board meetings
The director could be prevented from participating in the decision making process for both quorum and voting purposes at both board and shareholder meetings
The director could be prevented from participating in the decision making process for both quorum and voting purposes at board meetings
The director could be prevented from participating in the decision making process for both quorum and voting purposes at shareholder meetings
The director could be prevented from participating in the decision making process for voting purposes at shareholder meetings

explanation.en: The best answer is C. The director has a direct interest in the proposed purchase of the car from XYZ Limited. Article 14 could prevent the director from participating in the decision making process for both quorum and voting purposes at board meetings. Answer A is partially correct as it only considers quorum, but fails to specify voting rights. A shareholder is allowed to act in their own self-interest and has no obligation to declare any interest in a proposed transaction. This differs from the director's duty to act in the best interests of the business as a whole, and thus avoid conflicts of interest. As such, answers B, D and E are all incorrect.

stem: Your client is a member of a private company with holdings and voting rights of 20% of the shares. At the general meeting, the chairman of the board who presides over the meeting calls for the election of two new directors and wishes to proceed to vote on the matter by a single resolution by a show of hands. Your client, who is opposing the proposed nomination, asks the chairman to hold a vote by poll. The articles of association of the company, however, contains a provision that all members' resolutions at a general meeting must be made by a written resolution or by a show of hands, if the chairman of the meeting decides so.
ask: What would you advise your client?

options.en: The chairman has the authority to call for a show of hands vote; therefore your client cannot do anything
The chairman must call for a vote by a poll
The election of a new director must be made by a written resolution of the company; therefore the chairman has no authority to call for a vote by a show of hands

A motion for the appointment of two or more persons as directors of the company by a single resolution at a general meeting, must not be made unless a resolution that it should be so made has first been agreed to unanimously by the members. Therefore, the chairman cannot call for a vote under these circumstances
Your client can force a vote by poll if more than 50% of the members join in a motion to hold a vote by poll

explanation.en: The best answer is B - the chairman must call for a vote by poll. Generally, a member will have one vote for each share he holds on a written resolution or one vote on a show of hands at a general meeting regardless of the number of shares held, unless a poll is called. If someone validly calls for a poll at a general meeting, then each member has one vote for each share that he holds. Under section 321 of the Companies Act, a provision of a company's articles excluding the right to demand a poll at a general meeting (such as in this case), is void. The chairman, therefore, must hold a vote by a poll as requested by your client. Note that option D is incorrect as this applies only to public companies only under section 160 of the Companies Act 2006, and not to private companies. It should be noted that a provision in the articles of association will be void if it says that a poll cannot be validly demanded by any five or more members having the right to vote on the resolution, or the holders (whether present in person or by proxy) of not less than 10% of the voting rights of all the members having the right to vote on the resolution (except on resolutions to elect a chair or to adjourn). So in this case, since the client has 20% of the voting rights, nothing in the articles of association can validly exclude his statutory right to call for a vote by a poll.

stem: An act of Parliament allows for certain groups of individuals to make decisions over parking arrangements, within their neighbourhoods. These groups have obtained considerable power and the government (which controls Parliament) now wants to remove the power and effectively scrap the act that gave them the power, in the first place.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the power of Parliament, through the government, to handle the situation?

options.en: Parliament cannot go back on an act, at all
Parliament cannot go back on an act, without a good reason such as an abuse of power by the neighbourhood groups
Parliament is free to create and remove laws
Provided the government discussed the matter with the neighbourhood groups through the local authorities, it could then remove the act through Parliament
The permission of the Monarch is necessary to remove an act of Parliament in that specific situation

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The government which controls Parliament can add or remove acts, at any point, through Parliament. The concept is referred to as parliamentary sovereignty and is a central element of the principles of the British constitution.

stem: A very controversial bill is being proposed by Parliament and there is considerable public pressure being placed on every step of the process to prevent the bill from becoming a law.
ask: Which of the following statements is the most accurate in relation to this proposed Act?

options.en: The monarch has the power not to grant Royal Assent to the bill; therefore, if the public could persuade the monarch to withhold the Royal Assent, this would block the bill
The public will vote on the issue on a referendum, as it is so controversial; the majority will rule
The public can demand the House of Lords to look at the provisions of the bill and, potentially, prevent the bill from becoming a law
If there are public policy grounds why the bill should not be allowed to become a law, then the public can oppose the bill by approaching the Parliament through a special procedure
The Justices of the Supreme Court can refuse to apply the bill, on public policy grounds, if it becomes a law

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The monarch has the power and can prevent a bill from becoming a law, by withholding or reserving Royal Assent. Public pressure may, therefore, impact on the decisions made during the passing of the act. It should be noted, however, that in reality this move may spark a constitutional and political crisis.

stem: Bob wishes to become Prime Minister and is, in fact, head of a political party that is likely to win the next election. Based on this, he believes that he is guaranteed the role.
ask: Which of the following is an accurate reflection of the legal position?

options.en: The Prime Minister is the head of the party who wins the election; so, if the public vote for his party, he becomes Prime Minister
The Prime Minister is the head of the party who wins the election; so, if the public vote for his party, he becomes Prime Minister. However, he will, ultimately, have to be appointed by the monarch
The members of the political group will have to vote for whom they want as a leader, once they have won the public vote
The level of support for the individual is irrelevant; essentially, it is the leader of the dominant party who becomes Prime Minister
Bob will automatically become Prime Minister if his party wins the elections

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Although, in practice, it is the leader of the winning party that becomes prime minister, the monarch still, ultimately, appoints the prime minister; the monarch will also look for an individual that commands the support of the House of Commons.

stem: A new monarch has just come to power and is much more involved in his political activity and is keen to use his Royal Prerogative. In doing so, the monarch decides to dismiss the Prime Minister and appoint a new one, declare war on a small island off the British coast, issue passports without question to a specific country that they like, change the British flag and change the structure of the armed forces. Several public individuals are concerned that the monarch is acting irresponsibly and asks for your advice.
ask: What is the legal position?

options.en: The Royal Prerogative is constitutionally unlimited, so the monarch has the ultimate power and they can do what they want
The monarch can do anything that relates to the management of the UK; so, they can change the armed forces, the flag and the Prime Minister, but they cannot declare war and issue passports
The monarch has to obtain the permission of the Prime Minister to make these changes

The monarch can make all of the changes, with the exception of declaring war. However, there is a debate as to the limitation of powers of the monarch and to what extent they are subject to judicial review

The monarch can make all of the changes, with the exception of changing the flag. However, there is a debate as to the limitation of powers of the monarch and to what extent they are subject to judicial review

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The Royal Prerogative is relatively broad and has never been formally written out in a document; however, the power to change the flag has not been stated as being part of the Royal Prerogative; all other changes are within the power of the monarch, exclusively.

stem: A group of powerful politicians has been involved in a range of activities that are contrary to several acts of Parliament. There are also activities being undertaken that, although not illegal, are clearly against the general principles of the law. The public interest group is not happy with the behaviours of the politicians (one of whom is the Prime Minister) and asks for your advice.
ask: Which of the following is the closest reflection of the position?

options.en: The Prime Minister and the politicians are both subject to the actual laws themselves, but not to any unspoken rules that have not been enacted into law
If the politicians were acting in accordance with their roles, then they cannot be subject to additional laws controlling their civilian behaviour
The politicians are subject to all laws and also any general principles, but the Prime Minister has greater flexibility with his behaviour
The politicians are subject to the actual laws, but do not need to be concerned about principles that have not actually been brought into law; the Prime Minister is immune
The Prime Minister is subject to the actual laws and the general principles; the politicians are only subject to the actual laws

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. In accordance with the rule of law, no one is above the law, including the Prime Minister and it must be applied, equally, to all people. If the rules have not been brought into law, then the individuals cannot be subject to them and therefore only the actual laws will apply.

stem: One of your clients is particularly concerned about a bill that has been proposed, as it would place substantial restrictions on his business, to the extent that he will probably not have a business, should this bill be enacted. He asks you for a description of the process that this bill will go through, before becoming enacted.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate response?

options.en: The bill will be read by the House of Commons, firstly, and will then go straight to House of Lords to be enacted
A committee will analyse the bill, on a clause by clause basis
The House of Lords has an absolute option to reject a bill
The House of Commons can send a bill to the House of Lords, at any time during an active session
The public will get a chance to vote

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. As part of the process, the committee will look at the bill, clause by clause, and report back to the House of Commons. The House of Commons must send the bill to the House of Lords, once it is satisfied with it, no less than a month before the end of session.

stem: Following many events which have resulted in concerns that the government is being overbearing, during the passage of several bills, one of your clients is looking at the constitutional position to establish whom the government is answerable to and what can be done about these concerns.
ask: What do you tell the client?

options.en: The government is answerable to the public
The government is answerable to the House of Lords
The government is answerable to the House of Commons
The government is answerable to the monarch
The government is answerable to no-one

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The government is answerable to the House of Commons and, whilst it may also be required to answer to other bodies, for example, the House of Lords may question the government at question time; ultimately, however, it is answerable to the House of Commons.

stem: The Act of Union 1801 created a single British Parliament within the entire British Isles. This meant that until the recent devolution of power to regional legislatures in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, that the seat of Westminster remained the sole legislative body for the people of mainland Britain.
ask: Which entity did the Act of Union 1801 create?

options.en: The Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
The Kingdom of Great Britain
The British Empire

explanation.en: B is correct. The Act of Union 1801 created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

stem: Jemima Hacker has just been appointed Secretary of State for the Department of Administrative Affairs. She is due to meet the Permanent Secretary for the Department of Administrative Affairs, Dame Caroline Appleby. Jemima Hacker is unsure, however, what the characteristics and role of the Civil Service should be.
ask: As a civil servant to the minister, which qualities should Dame Caroline observe?

options.en: Political professionalism and perspicacity
Political competence and cordiality
Political initiative and organisation
Political correctness and caution
Political neutrality and integrity

explanation.en: E is correct. The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 puts the Civil Service Commission on a statutory footing, confers on the Minister for the Civil Service the power to manage the civil service, requires the Minister to publish a code of conduct for the civil service and sets out some minimum requirements for the code (including obligations of political impartiality, integrity, honesty, etc...). Statute; rule; constitution: The Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: The role of Lord Chancellor had been called in to question regarding the constitutional separation of powers. Rather than the complete abolition of the post of Lord Chancellor, however, the previous government took the opportunity to make fundamental changes to the Lord Chancellor's role. In this respect, the Lord Chancellor retains an important executive role.
ask: Which one of the following is a true statement of a key role of the Lord Chancellor'?

options.en: Head of the judiciary
Judicial appointments
The Lord Speaker
Justice Secretary
Judge

explanation.en: D is correct. The Lord Chancellor is a member of the Cabinet and the executive functions of his Department are now to be found in the Ministry of Justice. The Secretary of State for Justice is also Lord Chancellor. Statute; rule; constitution: The Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: The State Opening of Parliament marks the beginning of the parliamentary session. On such occasions, the Queen, accompanied by her husband the Duke of Edinburgh, steps out of her carriage at Westminster. The Queen arrives at Parliament, takes her speech from the Lord Chancellor, and delivers it from the Throne in the House of Lords, in the presence of Members of both Houses.
ask: Who is ultimately responsible for preparing the Queen's speech?

options.en: The Speaker of the House
The Government
The Lord Chancellor
. The Sovereign
The Prime Minister

explanation.en: B is correct. Although the Queen reads the Speech, the content is entirely drawn up by the Government and approved by the Cabinet.

stem: Under the unwritten British Constitution, there are two important conventions which help to preserve judicial independence. The first is that Parliament does not criticise or comment on the cases which are before the court (as well as ministers who do not criticise judges). The second is the principle of parliamentary privilege.
ask: Which key function is served by parliamentary privilege?

options.en: It serves as recompense for the Members of House's travel and stay-over expenses when they must attend proceedings in the capital
It guarantees that the separation of powers is preserved and effectively upheld
It is of Parliamentary historical curiosity but no longer serves any real contemporary function
It gives the members of Parliament the right to say what they will and discuss what they will
It protects free debate in Parliament in the public interest, as long as defamatory words naming individuals to do not contravene the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR)

explanation.en: D is correct. Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689 recognises and enshrines a longstanding privilege of Parliament: freedom of speech and debate. It is an absolute privilege and is of the highest constitutional importance. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 9 Bill of Rights 1689.

stem: The Scottish Parliament is located in Edinburgh. The Welsh Assembly is based in Cardiff. The Northern Ireland Assembly is based in Belfast.
ask: Where is the English Parliament located?

options.en: London
Parliament
Westminster
The House of Commons
England doesn't have its own Parliament

explanation.en: E is correct. England doesn't have its own Parliament. It is the only country in the UK not to have a devolved national legislature. In the island of Britain today there are three governments representing three constitutional and political bodies. There is the Scottish Parliament, there is the Welsh Assembly, there is the United Kingdom Parliament. They represent Scotland, Wales and the United Kingdom. Constitutionally and politically just those three exist. Constitutionally and politically England does not exist. That situation, and its implications, constitutes the English Question.

stem: A bill to extend the term of the MP membership to seven years was originated in the House of Commons. The bill was debated among the MPs, as some argued it may be non- constitutional, however eventually the bill was passed by the Lower House.
ask: Which of the following best described the legal position?

options.en: The bill has no effect and is unconstitutional. Membership of MPs cannot be longer than five years
The bill will come into effect and will become an act when Royal Assent is granted
The bill will come into effect as a law if approved by the House of Lords and a Royal Assent is granted
The bill has no effect as it had to be originated by the House of Lords
The bill will come into effect as a law if approved by the House of Lords

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The Parliament Act 1911 removed from the House of Lords the power to veto a Bill, except one to extend the lifetime of a Parliament. Therefore, a bill that seeks to extend a parliamentary term beyond five years requires the consent of the House of Lords.

stem: A Member of Parliament has proposed to introduce a new football tax, at the rate of 5% which will be added to the regular ticket price of football games. The MP introduced a Public Bill for debate before the House of Commons, who voted in favour. The bill was then also presented to the House of Lords which decided to amend the bill and reduce the tax rate to 2%. The House of Lords then voted in favour of the amended bill.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The House of Commons is responsible for making decisions on financial Bills, such as proposed new taxes. The House of Lords can consider these Bills but cannot block or amend them
The bill will return to the House of Commons for reconsideration, and if approved at the new rate, it could then be sent directly to the Monarch for approval
The House of Commons is responsible for making decisions on financial Bills, such as proposed new taxes. The House of Lords can consider these Bills but can only block and not amend them

The House of Commons is responsible for making decisions on financial Bills, such as proposed new taxes. The House of Lords can consider these Bills and can amend them, as opposed to block them. Therefore once a Royal Assent will be given the bill will become am Act
The House of Commons and the House of Lords must both approve the bill on the same terms

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The House of Commons alone is responsible for making decisions on financial Bills, such as proposed new taxes. The House of Lords can consider these Bills but cannot block or amend them, but the House of Commons often waives its privileges and allows the Lords to make amendments with financial implications.

stem: A bill that prohibits UK citizen from leaving their homes after 9.00pm due to increased violence at nights is passed by the Parliament and put forward to the Sovereign for Royal Assent. The Sovereign believes that the bill may be unconstitutional.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the monarch's constitutional position?

options.en: The Sovereign must refuse to give the Bill Royal Assent due to public safety considerations
The Sovereign must give the Bill Royal Assent
The Sovereign may reserve the Royal Assent and defer a decision on the bill until a later time
The monarch must return the Bill to Parliament for a further reading
If the monarch refuses to give the Bill Royal Assent Parliament has power to pass the Bill into law due to public safety

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Once a bill is presented to the Sovereign or the Sovereign's representative, he or she has three formal options: 1) The Sovereign may grant the Royal Assent, thereby making the bill an Act of Parliament. 2) The Sovereign may withhold the Royal Assent, thereby vetoing the bill. 3) The Sovereign may reserve the Royal Assent and defer a decision on the bill until a later time.

stem: The Prime Minister has drawn up a list of people to be honoured with a peerage for the New Year. Mr. X's name was raised as a candidate to be appointed to the House of Lords.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position of his nomination?

options.en: Mr. X can be appointed as a Lord Spiritual for life by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister
Mr. X can be appointed as a Lord Temporal for life by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister
Mr. X can be appointed as a Lord Spiritual for five years by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister
Mr. X can be appointed as a Lord Spiritual for ten years by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister
Mr. X can be appointed as a Lord Temporal for life by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister and approval of the House of Lords

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The majority of the Lords Temporal are life peers who are appointed by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister. Lite peers hold their title for the duration of their lifetimes and the title becomes redundant on the death of the holder.

stem: Several months after the general elections, one of the MPs of the largest party in the House of Commons dies in a car accident. The Prime Minister has asked the Parliament to approve the nomination of Mr. New MP.
ask: What would you advise him?

options.en: The Prime Minister can appoint Mr. New MP as a Member of the Parliament instead of the deceased MP
The Prime Minister can appoint Mr. New MP as a Member of Parliament instead of the deceased MP if his nomination is approved by the majority of the MPs
The Prime Minister cannot appoint Mr. New MP as a Member of Parliament instead of the deceased MP, unless the nomination is approved by the Sovereign
The Prime Minister cannot appoint Mr. New MP as a Member of Parliament instead of the deceased MP
The Prime Minister cannot appoint Mr. New MP as a Member of Parliament instead of the deceased MP, unless both Houses approve the nomination

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The Prime Minister cannot appoint Mr. New MP instead of the deceased MP. Once elected, Members of Parliament normally continue to serve until the next dissolution of Parliament. If a Member, however, dies or ceases to be qualified, his or her seat falls vacant and is not replaced by the Prime Minister. S vacancy may be filled by a by- election in the appropriate constituency, with the same electoral system as in general elections.

stem: One of the Members of Parliament is accused of accepting a bribe of £50,000. The others Members of his Party would like to expel the Member from the Parliament and ask for your advice.
ask: What would you tell them?

options.en: They cannot do anything; Members of Parliament are immune from any prosecution and serve until the next dissolution of Parliament
The House of Commons can expel a Member, in certain circumstances, and his seat will fall vacant
The House of Commons can expel a Member, in certain circumstances, and his seat may be filled by a by-election in the appropriate constituency
The House of Commons cannot expel a Member, in certain circumstances, unless the Sovereign has approved it. In such case and his seat will fall vacant
The House of Commons must expel a Member that is involved in criminal activity and his seat may be filled by a by-election in the appropriate constituency

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. They hold their seats until Parliament is dissolved (a maximum of five years after the preceding election). Once elected, Members of Parliament normally continue to serve until the next dissolution of Parliament. If a Member, however, dies or ceases to be qualified, his or her seat falls vacant. It is also possible for the House of Commons to expel a Member, but this power is exercised only in cases of serious misconduct or criminal activity. In each case, a vacancy may be filled by a by-election in the appropriate constituency (electoral district), with the same electoral system as in general elections.

stem: A Money Bill has been passed by the House of Commons and has sent it to the House of Lords for approval five weeks before the end of session. With less than three days to go before end of session it still has not been heard.
ask: What is the legal position?

options.en: There is nothing that the House of Commons can do, the House of Lords approval is necessary for a Money Bill
The House of Lords would have a period of 12 months to hear the Money Bill so it will have to wait for the next session
The House of Commons can apply to the monarch for the House of Lords to be circumnavigated
As it s a Money Bill and it has been presented with a month free before the end of the session it can go straight for Royal Assent if the House of Lords fail to pass the bill
The House of Commons can hold a vote and if they have a majority in favour it can be passed without the House of Lords

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. If a Money Bill, having been passed by the House of Commons, and sent up to the House of Lords at least one month betore the end of the session, is not passed by the House of Lords without amendment within one month after it is so sent up to that House, the Bill shall, unless the House of Commons direct to the contrary, be present to His Majesty and become an Act of Parliament on the Royal Assent being signified, notwithstanding that the House of Lords have not consented to the Bill.

stem: After a particularly stressful few months the Prime Minister has resigned. You are asked to advise the sovereign as to what should now happen.
ask: What do you advise the sovereign?

options.en: The deputy prime minister is automatically appointed
The public need to be asked in an election
The sovereign can appoint whoever they want
The sovereign would need to appoint the most appropriate person who is likely to gain the majority support
It's up to the outgoing prime minister to choose their successor

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Whenever the office of prime minister falls vacant, the Sovereign appoints the person who has the support of the House, or who is most likely to command the support of the House — normally the leader of the largest party in the Commons (The leader of the second-largest party becomes the Leader of the Opposition). A prime minister may resign even if he or she is not defeated at the polls (for example, for personal health reasons); in such a case, the premiership goes to whoever can command a majority in the House of Commons, in practice this is usually the new leader of the outgoing prime minister's party.

stem: A few weeks after the victory of his party in the elections, Mr. V. as the leader of the largest party in the House of Common was appointed as the new Prime Minister of the government by the Sovereign. The Prime Minister would like to appoint the ministers and select the members of the Cabinet.
ask: Which of the following statement best describes the legal position?

options.en: The Prime Minister has the power to appoint ministers to the government and the Cabinet, with the approval of the Sovereign
The Prime Minister has the power to appoint ministers to the government but not the Cabinet, with the approval of the Sovereign
The Prime Minister does not have the power to appoint ministers either to the government or to the Cabinet
The Prime Minister has the power to appoint ministers to the Cabinet but not to the government
The Prime Minister has the power to appoint ministers to the Cabinet but not the government, as soon as his appointment takes effect after the formal vote in the House of Commons

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The government of the United Kingdom is led by the Prime Minister, who is appointed by the Sovereign. The Sovereign appoints and dismisses other ministers on the advice of the Prime Minister (and such appointments and dismissals occur quite frequently as part of cabinet reshuffles). The Prime Minister selects the most senior Ministers to the supreme decision-making committee, known as the Cabinet. The Cabinet members advise the monarch as members of the Privy Council. The Prime Minister and all other ministers take office immediately upon appointment by the Sovereign. In the United Kingdom, unlike many other countries, there is no requirement for a formal vote of approval by the legislature either of the Government as a whole or of its individual members before they may assume office.

stem: Foreign nationals challenged a decision of the Special Immigration Appeals Commission to deport them from the country on the basis that there was evidence of them being a threat to national security. All were detained under anti-terrorism legislation.
ask: Which one of the following is a true statement in respect of discretionary powers?

options.en: Where the prerogative is a discretionary power to be exercised for the public good, it follows that its exercise cannot be examined by the courts when a matter of national security or state necessity is concerned

The judiciary must in general defer to the executive's assessment of what constitutes a threat to national security or to the life of the nation, but such deference should not be blindly extended, irrespective of the likely quality of such executive assessments
The chief responsibility of protecting national security sits on the shoulders of the judiciary
As far as national security is concerned, the courts will not intervene when Parliament and ministers execute their functions
Indefinite imprisonment without charge is not contrary to the rule of law where the detained person poses an acute threat to national security
