explanation.en: B is correct. Courts will accord to Parliament and ministers, as the primary decision-makers, an appropriate degree of latitude. The courts will intervene only when it is apparent that, in balancing the various considerations involved, the primary decision - maker must have given insufficient weight to the human rights factor. Lead case: A and others v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 56.

stem: According to Dicey, the Rule of Law, as he formulated it, was a principle of the English Constitution. He asserted that "Englishmen are ruled by the law, and by the law alone; a man may with us be punished for a breach of law, but he can be punished for nothing else".
ask: Which one of the following statements is true in respect of Dicey's formulation of the Rule of Law?

options.en: The rule of law is the same as social justice
The law must prevail over arbitrariness and discretionary power
The rule of law is another form of political control
The separation of powers constitutes the rule of law
The executive always acts in the public interest

explanation.en: B is correct. Dicey stated that the rule of law, "means, in the first place, the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power, and excludes the existence of arbitrariness, of prerogative, or even of wide discretionary authority on the part of the government".

stem: The separation of powers, together with the rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty, runs like a thread throughout the constitution of the United Kingdom. It is a doctrine which is fundamental to the organization of a state and to the concept of constitutionalism.
ask: Which one of the following statements is true in respect of this formulation of the Separation of Powers?

options.en: The judicial arm of government is chiefly responsible for creating, undoing, and amending the law
Parliament is subordinate to the judicial arm of the constitution
The judiciary creates and enforces the law
The chief burden upon the executive is to interpret and apply the law, resolve disputes, provide remedies, and determine punishments when the law is breached
The separation of powers is a constitutional principle designed to ensure that the functions, personnel and powers of the major institutions of the state are not concentrated in any one body

explanation.en: E is correct. The separation of powers is a constitutional principle designed to ensure that the functions, personnel and powers of the major institutions of the state are not concentrated in any one body. The British Constitution, though largely unwritten, is firmly based on the separation of powers; Parliament makes the laws, the judiciary interpret them. There is no absolute formal separation of the principal constitutional organs—Parliament, Crown and Cabinet and the judiciary — so that the personnel of each are kept rigidly distinct with no overlap. As Bagehot wrote in The English Constitution (1867): "The efficient secret of the English Constitution may be described as the close union, the nearly complete fusion of the executive and legislative powers'.

stem: The doctrine of the separation of powers is that the whole power of one branch of government should not be exercised by the same hands which possess the whole power of either of the other branches. Such exercise of the whole would subvert the principles of the doctrine.
ask: Which one of the following statements is true in respect of this formulation of the Separation of Powers?

options.en: Although the executive proposes legislation, only Parliament may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals
Although Parliament proposes legislation, only the executive may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals
Although Parliament proposes legislation, only the judiciary may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals
Although the judiciary proposes legislation, only Parliament may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals
Although the executive proposes legislation, only the judiciary may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals

explanation.en: A is correct. The government proposes legislation: only Parliament, however, may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals. While there is no formal separation of the powers of the legislature and executive and while legislative authority is vested in the Sovereign in Parliament, it is a constitutional convention that the government proposes, and Parliament disposes. Parliament is charged with fulfilling two core functions: supporting and scrutinizing the executive.

stem: One of the fundamental principles of the British constitution is the doctrine of the separation of powers, which was first put forward by the 18th century French philosopher Montesquieu. Under this model, the state is divided into three branches, each with separate and independent powers and an area of responsibility. No branch has more power than the other branches and each branch checks and balances the others.
ask: Which one of the following statements is true regarding checks and balances under the separation of powers?

options.en: Parliament's right to make whatever laws it chooses is challengeable under the separation of powers
The judiciary in Parliament enables scrutiny of the judiciary, as long as the necessary procedures are in place
The judiciary in Parliament plays an administrative role in governing the country
The executive in Parliament enables scrutiny of the executive, as long as the necessary procedures are in place
Parliament in the executive enables scrutiny of Parliament, as long as the necessary procedures are in place

explanation.en: D is correct. The three branches of government overlap, as most obviously in the case of the executive sitting in Parliament. In the case of the executive in Parliament, this clearly facilitates scrutiny of the executive, provided that the necessary procedures are in place.

stem: In the absence of a written constitution, the issue that requires evaluation is the manner in which and the extent to which differing functions are kept separate. For the purpose of analysis, the subject may be further broken down by considering the extent to which the executive and legislature, executive and judiciary, and judiciary and legislature overlap and interact.
ask: Which one of the following statements is a true reflection of how the separation of powers is ensured in the UK constitution?

options.en: Parliament's right to make whatever laws it chooses is challengeable under the separation of powers
Although Parliament proposes legislation, only the executive may enact laws which give legal effect to these proposals
Government ministers must uphold the independence of the judiciary, barring them from trying to influence judicial decisions by special access to judges
The judiciary must uphold the independence of government ministers, by creating, undoing, and amending the law
The chief burden upon the executive is to interpret and apply the law, resolve disputes, provide remedies, and determine punishments when the law is breached

explanation.en: C is correct. The independence of the judiciary is guaranteed by the Constitutional Reform Act 2005. Ministers have a statutory duty to uphold the independence of the judiciary under the Act. Statute; rule; constitution: The Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: The story of the UK's constitutional is one more of evolution than revolution. First there was the gradual unification of disparate kingdoms under one national sovereign, or monarch. Then came the struggle for supremacy between the sovereign and the Christian Church, and ultimately between the sovereign and Parliament.
ask: Which one of the following statements is a true reflection of the place of the monarch in Britain?

options.en: The UK has a constitutional monarchy
As a constitutional monarchy, the country is ruled by the Sovereign
The monarch may sit as a judge in the Supreme Court
The monarch may raise an army without Parliament's consent
The monarch may sit in the House of Commons

explanation.en: A is correct. The UK is a constitutional monarchy. As a Constitutional Monarch, the Queen does not 'rule' the country and is limited to non-partisan functions.

stem: The Act of Settlement is described as the backbone of the British constitution. Under the Act, the monarch must join in communion with the Church of England, must declare him or herself to be a Protestant, and must swear to maintain the established churches in England and Scotland and take the coronation oath.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position, if the monarch wishes to retain the title to the throne but marry a non-Protestant?

options.en: The monarch is barred from marrying a Jew
The monarch is not barred from marrying a Roman Catholic
The monarch is not barred from being a Roman Catholic
The monarch is barred from marrying a Roman Catholic
The monarch is barred from marrying an atheist

explanation.en: B is correct. The monarch is not barred from marrying a Roman Catholic. Under the Succession to the Crown Act 2013, a person is not disqualified from succeeding to the Crown or from possessing it as a result of marrying a person of the Roman Catholic faith. However the Monarch must be a Protestant and cannot be a Roman Catholic. Statute; rule; constitution: Succession to the Crown Act 2013.

stem: On the death of the reigning monarch, the person entitled to succeed to the throne does so as soon as his or her predecessor dies, as summed up in the phrase: "The King is dead; long live the King!" The new Sovereign is proclaimed as soon as possible at an Accession Council.
ask: Which legal maxim of common law does this process of accession give rise to?

options.en: The monarch can do no wrong
The monarch is the dignified part rather than the efficient part of government
The monarch is primus inter pares (first among equals)
The monarch is above the law
The monarch never dies

explanation.en: E is correct. The maxim of common law is that 'the King never dies'. The title to the crown derives partly trom statute and partly from common law rules of descent. The sovereign succeeds to the throne as soon as his or her predecessor dies. He or she is at once proclaimed at an Accession Council, to which all members of the Privy Council are called. Members of the House of Lords, the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and other leading citizens of the City of London are also invited. The coronation follows the accession. The ceremony takes place at Westminster Abbey in London in the presence of representatives of both Houses of Parliament and all the major public organisations in the UK. The prime ministers and leading members of the Commonwealth nations and representatives of other countries also attend. Comment: See Halsbury's LawsVol 8(2) para 40 (see footnote 2).

stem: Prerogative powers can provide flexibility in dealing with specific or exceptional circumstances that are not covered by statutory provisions. They provide a basis on which governments may act outside the framework of Acts of Parliament.
ask: Which one of the following statements is true in respect of the relationship between royal prerogative and statute?

options.en: Where statutory provisions and prerogative powers act in the same area, the prerogative power prevails over the statutory provisions
Where statutory provisions and prerogative powers act in the same area, the prerogative power cannot not be used contrary to the provisions
The executive can use the royal prerogative to achieve something which is inconsistent with a statutory scheme if it is in the public interest to do so
The executive can use the royal prerogative to pre-empt an Act of Parliament, even if this conflicts with Parliament's wishes
The Crown is not bound by any constraints, limitations, and provisions passed by Act of Parliament

explanation.en: B is correct. Where statutory provisions and prerogative powers act in the same area, the prerogative power cannot not be used contrary to the provisions. There have been several influential decisions of the House of Lords which have seriously limited the use of prerogatives. The principle of statutory superiority (the case of Keyser's Royal Hotel Ltd.) was extended in Laker Airways Ltd v Department of Trade, where it was confirmed that prerogative powers could not be used to contradict a statutory provision, and that in situations where the power and the statute were designed to be used side by side, the power could only be used to further the aim of the statute. Another extension came with R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Fire Brigades Union, where the Court of Appeal held that even if a statute had not yet come into force, the prerogative could not be used to alter this statute to "conflict with Parliament's wishes". Lead case: Attorney-General v De Keyser's Royal Hotel Limited [1920] AC 75.

stem: The Supreme Court ruled that compensation was payable to English Petroleum after its Libyan assets had been destroyed during war time in order to prevent it from falling into Colonel Gadaffi's hands. The government quickly proposed and Parliament passed the War Damage Act 2011 which effectively quashed the decision.
ask: Which one of the following statements is the most relevant in respect of Parliamentary Sovereignty?

options.en: The separation of powers is a constitutional principle designed to ensure that the functions, personnel and powers of the major institutions of the state are concentrated in the hands of Parliament
Parliament is subordinate to the judicial arm of the constitution in England
Parliament can overturn the effect of judicial decisions prospectively
Parliament cannot overturn the effect of judicial decisions retrospectively
Parliament can overturn the effect of judicial decisions retrospectively

explanation.en: E is correct. Parliament can overturn the effect of judicial decisions retrospectively. Burmah Oil v Lord Advocate (1965) was concerned with the destruction of oil fields in Burma by British forces during the Second World War. The sabotage was committed in order to prevent the plantations from falling into the hands of the advancing Japanese army. The House of Lords held, by majority, that although the damage was lawful, it was the equivalent of requisitioning the property. Any act of requisition was done for the good of the public, at the expense of the individual proprietor, and for that reason, the company was entitled to damages from the State. The House of Lords ordered the government to pay compensation to Burmah Oil Company, but the decision was frustrated by the passing of a retrospective Act of Parliament, the War Damage Act 1965, which retroactively exempts the Crown from liability in respect of damage to, or destruction of, property caused by acts lawfully done by the Crown during, or in contemplation of the outbreak of, a war in which it is engaged. Lead case: Burma Oil Company v Lord Advocate [1965] AC 75.

stem: The government enacted a law which attempted to cement the status of Cornwall within the United Kingdom as long as its people desired this arrangement. Article 10 of the Cornwall Act of Union stated: "... no alteration be made in laws which concern private right except for the evident utility of the people of Cornwall" and other Articles expressly preserve the Cornish Church, Education, and Legal System.
ask: Which one of the following statements is the most relevant in respect of Parliamentary Sovereignty?

options.en: The Cornwall Act of Union is an example of the enrolled bill rule principle in action
The Cornwall Act of Union is an example of implied repeal in action
The Cornwall Act of Union is an example of the doctrine of manner or form in action
The Cornwall Act of Union is an example of entrenchment in action
The Cornwall Act of Union is an example of parliamentary privilege in action

explanation.en: D is correct. An example of entrenchment in action is the Northern Ireland Constitution (Amendment) Act 1973, and subsequent Acts and agreements, which attempted to entrench the status of Northern Ireland within the United Kingdom as long as its people preferred this and to give the Republic of Ireland a mechanism to represent its views on aspects of Northern Ireland

stem: An alien was to be removed from the UK while his case was considered by the court. The Home Secretary gave an undertaking to the court that this would not happen until after the hearing of the appeal. Nevertheless, before the hearing of the appeal, the alien was eventually deported from the country.
ask: Which one of the following statements is one of the key features of government according to the rule of law?

options.en: The law cannot be enforced by the courts against a minister of the Crown acting in his official capacity
The law can be enforced by the courts against a minister of the Crown acting in his official capacity
A public body exercising statutory duties is not obliged to undertake what statute requires it to do
The courts are duty bound to correct any abuse of power by Parliament and the judges are free to exercise this jurisdiction independently
The judiciary is barred from enforcing the law against ministers of the executive

explanation.en: B is correct. The law can be enforced by the courts against a minister of the Crown acting in his official capacity. In M v Home Office (1993) the Home Secretary was liable in contempt of court for removal in breach of undertaking. Lead case: M v Home Office (1993) 3 WLR 433.

stem: Armed police broke into the home of a suspected terrorist and seized his private papers. The suspected terrorist was arrested for possessing 'subversive' written material, a crime that is neither on the statute books nor part of the common law. The police were acting on the orders of the Home Secretary (a government minister responsible for national security).
ask: Which one of the following statements is one of the key features of government according to the rule of law?

options.en: The Home Secretary acts in the public interest when he takes pre-emptive action to avoid potential criminal activities
The Home Secretary was acting in the public interest because state necessity is a defence to an action in the tort of trespass
The suspect will succeed in an action because the main issue under the constitutional principle of the rule of law is that of the tort of trespass
If the police claim to have the power to do something they must be able to identify the precise legal source of its powers
The judiciary is barred from enforcing the law against ministers of the executive

explanation.en: D is correct. The executive can do nothing without legal authority. Where a public authority claims to have the power to do something it must be able to identify the precise legal source of its powers. Please note, while with the ratio of the case of Entick v Carrington (1765) concerns whether state necessity can be used as a defence to an action in the tort of trespass, this is not the relevant principle regarding the rule of law. Lead case: Entick v Carrington (1765).

stem: In the 17th century, disputes arose over the undefined residue of prerogative power claimed by the Stuart kings. The conflict was resolved only after the execution of one King and the expulsion of another in 1649 (Charles I) and 1688 (James II), culminating in the Bill of Rights 1689.
ask: Which of the following statements best exemplifies an historical royal prerogative that is still in operation?

options.en: An example of historical royal prerogative that is still in operation is Corpus Delicti
An example of historical royal prerogative that is still in operation is Habeas Corpus
An example of historical royal prerogative that is still in operation is Locus Standi
An example of historical royal prerogative that is still in operation is Primus Inter Pares
An example of historical royal prerogative that is still in operation is Ultra Vires

explanation.en: B is correct. An example of historical royal prerogative is "Habeas corpus" (Latin meaning "you are to have the body", i.e. "you should arrest"), which is a prerogative writ, used to challenge the validity of a person's detention, either in official custody or in private hands. Nexi Question

stem: Most primary legislation passed by Parliament originates from bills introduced by the government. There are, however, a number of procedures whereby Private Members and ordinary Members of Parliament (MPs) may initiate bills and ultimately pass legislation.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of Private Members' Bills?

options.en: Private Members' Bills are Private Bills introduced by MPs and Lords who aren't government ministers
Private Members' Bills are Private Bills introduced by MPs who aren't government ministers
Private Members' Bills are Private Bills introduced by Lords who aren't government ministers
Private Members' Bills are Public Bills introduced by MPs and Lords who aren't government ministers
Private Members' Bills are proposals for a law that would apply to a particular individual or group of individuals, or corporate entity

explanation.en: D is correct. Private Members' Bills are Public Bills introduced by MPs and Lords who aren't government ministers. As with other Public Bills their purpose is to change the law as it applies to the general population. A minority of Private Members' Bills become law but, by creating publicity around an issue, they may affect legislation indirectly.

stem: Despite enormous upheavals over the centuries, the reigning Sovereign still holds key constitutional offices. These are actual prerogative powers, exercised by the Monarch.
ask: Which of the following is one of the key constitutional offices still held by the Monarch?

options.en: Source of the Royal Mint's authority
Head of the Catholic Church in England
Lord Speaker of Parliament
Head of the Judiciary of England and Wales
Supreme functionary in the Government of the United Kingdom

explanation.en: A is correct. General prerogative powers include various other historic powers relating to such things as royal charters, mining precious metals, coinage, franchises for markets, treasure trove, printing, guardianship of infants.

stem: Government Bills embody government policy and a Minister introduces them. The bulk of Parliament's time is taken up with these types of bills. If the government has a large parliamentary majority, it is almost certain that all government Bills will be passed into law (though some may be amended along the way).
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of Public Bills in Parliament?

options.en: Public Bills affect the general public but also have a significant impact for specific individuals or groups
Public Bills are introduced to ensure that government Bills can get through the Lords when the government of the day has no majority in the Lords
Public Bills change the law as it applies to the general population
Public Bills are introduced for the purpose of being sent up to the Lords less than a month before the end of a session
Public bills are introduced to change the law as it applies to specific individuals or organisations

explanation.en: C is correct. Public Bills change the law as it applies to the general population (such as a change to the national speed limit on motorways). They deal with matters of public policy. Most are introduced to Parliament by the Government. They tend to be general in character and affect everyone.

stem: The 1689 Bill of Rights does not constitute what is generally understood as a modern "bill of rights", if by that term one means a document which defines and guarantees the basic human rights of individual citizens. Nor is it, on its own, the equivalent of a written constitution, although it can be viewed as a watershed in the development of the British constitution and especially with regard to the role of parliament.
ask: Which of the following statements best illustrates how the Bill of Rights is still in operation today?

options.en: The Bill of Rights 1689 prescribes the limits of executive power in English law; namely that an officer of the state can only act lawfully in a manner prescribed by statute or common law
The Bill of Rights 1689 protects Members' rights of free speech in Parliament
The Bill of Rights 1689 prescribes specific liberties of the subject that the Crown is prohibited from infringing
The Bill of Rights 1689 prescribes further limits on the Crown by better securing the rights and liberties of the subject
The Bill of Rights 1689 introduced wide-ranging changes to the electoral system designed to take effectual measures for correcting abuses that had long prevailed in Parliament

explanation.en: B is correct. Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689 protects Members of Parliament's rights of free speech in Parliament. The Bill of Rights 1689 introduced a constitutional principle that is fundamental to the functioning of the British Parliament. Often incorrectly described as a convention, this product of statute, parliamentary privilege enabled any member of either chamber in Parliament to make accusations about individuals or companies in open debate without fear of arrest for contempt of court or of prosecution for defamation. Statute; rule; constitution: Article 9 Bill of Rights 1689.

stem: The powers of the House of Lords are limited by a combination of law and convention. The Parliament Acts, although rarely used, provide a way of solving disagreement between the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes a Bill which is subject to the Parliament Acts and need not be approved by the House Lords?

options.en: A Bill subject to the Parliament Acts which need not be approved by the House Lords is a Money Bill
A Bill subject to the Parliament Acts which need not be approved by the House Lords is a Private Bill
A Bill subject to the Parliament Acts which need not be approved by the House Lords is a Bill sent up to the Lords less than a month before the end of a session
A Bill subject to the Parliament Acts which need not be approved by the House Lords is a Bill which start in the Lords
A Bill subject to the Parliament Acts which need not be approved by the House Lords is a Bill to prolong the length of a Parliament beyond five years

explanation.en: A is correct. Some Bills are not subject to the Parliament Acts and must be approved by the House Lords: Bills prolonging the length of a Parliament beyond five years Private Bills Bills sent up to the Lords less than a month before the end of a session Bills which start in the Lords. Statute; rule; constitution: Parliament Act 1911/Parliament Act 1949.

stem: The Prime Minister (PM) is arguably the most important person in British politics, appointing Cabinet Ministers and driving government policy. Concerns have been raised, however, that the role of the PM is becoming increasingly presidential. The implication is that this is undermining the traditional role of the PM in Cabinet.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet?

options.en: The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is E Pluribus Unum (from many, one)
The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is Fidei Defensor (Defender of the Faith)
The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is primus inter pares (first amongst equals)
The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is pro bono publico (for the public good)
The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is Maintiens le Droit (Maintain the Right)

explanation.en: C is correct. The traditional role of the Prime Minister in Cabinet is primus inter pares (first amongst equals). This means that though the PM is the chief-spokesperson for the government, around the Cabinet table there is equal discussion amongst colleagues. The coalition government with Conservative PM David Cameron and Lib Dem Deputy PM Nick Clegg sharing the Cabinet table with Conservative and Lib Dem colleagues is a classic example of the doctrine of primus inter pares in action.

stem: Except in certain limited circumstances, Private Bills have to be presented to Parliament on or before 27 November in each year. They were common in the nineteenth century, and were used for the construction of railways, docks, harbours, and gas and water systems. Many projects for the construction of works (tramways, railways, canals, harbours etc.) for which a private bill was formerly necessary are now legislated for by a system of Orders made under the Transport and Works Act 1992.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of Private Bills?

options.en: Private Bills affect the general public but also have a significant impact for specific individuals or groups
Private Bills are introduced to ensure that government Bills can get through the Lords when the government of the day has no majority in the Lords
Private Bills change the law as it applies to the general population
Private Bills are introduced for the purpose of being sent up to the Lords less than a month before the end of a session
Private bills are introduced only to change the law as it applies to specific individuals or organisations, rather than the general public

explanation.en: E is correct. Private Bills are usually promoted by organisations, like local authorities or private companies, to give themselves powers beyond, or in conflict with, the general law. Private Bills only change the law as it applies to specific individuals or organisations, rather than the general public.

stem: Governments have a tendency to dominate the legislative functions of Parliament, by using their in-built majority in the House of Commons. In practice, governments can pass any legislation (within reason) in the Commons they wish, unless there is major dissent by MPs in the governing party (hence Lord Hailsham's coining of the term "elective dictatorship" in 1976).
ask: In light of this statement, which of the following options best describes the components of the British legislature?

options.en: The components of the British legislature consist of: the Judiciary, the House of Lords and the House of Commons
The components of the British legislature consist of: the Lords Temporal, the House of Lords and the House of Commons
The components of the British legislature consist of: the Lord Speaker, the House of Lords and the House of Commons
The components of the British legislature consist of: the Lords Spiritual, the House of Lords and the House of Commons
The components of the British legislature consist of: the Monarch, the House of Lords and the House of Commons

explanation.en: E is correct. The components of the British legislature consist of: the Monarch, the House of Lords and the House of Commons. Note: While Royal Assent of the Monarch is required for all Bills to become law, and certain delegated legislation must be made by the Monarch by Order in Council, in practice, real legislative power is vested in the House of Commons, as the Monarch generally acts on the advice of the Prime Minister, and the powers of the House of Lords are limited.

stem: Humphrey Hacker has faithfully served as the Permanent Secretary for the Department of Administrative Affairs for almost two decades. Mr Hacker is in line for a knighthood and he will henceforth be referred to as 'Sir Humphrey'. His knighthood is to be conferred under general prerogative powers.
ask: Which one of the following statements best describes how prerogative powers are exercised?

options.en: The judiciary exercise the majority of the prerogative powers, either in their own right or through the advice they provide to the Queen, which she is bound constitutionally to follow
The Queen exercises the majority of the prerogative powers, either in her own right or through the advice she provides to government ministers, which she is bound constitutionally to follow
The Prime Minister exercises the majority of the prerogative powers, either in his own right or through the advice he provides to the Queen, which she is bound constitutionally to follow
Government ministers exercise the majority of the prerogative powers, either in their own right or through the advice they provide to the Queen, which she is bound constitutionally to follow
Civil servants exercise the majority of the prerogative powers, either in their own right or through the advice they provide to the Queen, which she is bound constitutionally to follow

explanation.en: D is correct. Originally the prerogative would have been exercised by the reigning Monarch. However, over time a distinction was drawn between the Monarch acting in his or her individual capacity and the powers possessed by the Monarch as an embodiment of the State. As the governance of the realm became more complex, power was devolved from the Monarch and exercised by his or her advisers. In modern times Government Ministers exercise the bulk of the prerogative powers, either in their own right or through the advice they provide to The Queen which she is constitutionally bound to follow.

stem: The judiciary must be made up of individuals who are qualified for appointment, and of the highest calibre. Candidates must earn and deserve their places on the bench, whether sitting as magistrates, as part timers or as Law Lords. To apply to become a judge, therefore, it is necessary to have the relevant legal qualification.
ask: What is the qualification route for a person to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court?

options.en: The person must have held high judicial office for a period of at least 2 years
The person must have held high judicial office for a period of at least 4 years
The person must have held high judicial office for a period of at least 6 years
The person must have held high judicial office for a period of at least 8 years
The person must have held high judicial office for a period of at least 10 years

explanation.en: A is correct. A person is qualified to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court if, at any time, he has held high judicial office, (i.e. the High Court, Court of Appeal, Northern Irish High Court or Court of Appeal, or Scottish Court of Session), for a period of at least 2 years. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 25 of the Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: The judiciary must be made up of individuals who are qualified for appointment, and of the highest calibre. Candidates must earn and deserve their places on the bench, whether sitting as magistrates, as part timers or as Law Lords. To apply to become a judge, therefore, it is necessary to have the relevant legal qualification.
ask: What is the qualification route for a person to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court?

options.en: The person must have been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 5 years
The person must have been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 2 years
The person must have been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 7 years
The person must have been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 10 years
The person must have been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 15 years

explanation.en: E is correct. A person is qualified to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court if, at any time, he has been a qualifying practitioner, for a period of at least 15 years. The statutory minimum qualification for appointment is to have held high judicial office for a period of at least two years, or to have satisfied the judicial appointment eligibility condition on a 15-year basis or to have been a qualifying practitioner for a period of at least 15 years. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 25 of the Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: A distinguished Lord Justice of the Court of Appeal's name has been suggested for appointment as a Justice of the Supreme Court. He is not sure which body or person has the right to appoint him to this honourable position.
ask: Which of the following statements represents the best advice that you can give him?

options.en: Appointments of Supreme Court Justices are made by the Lord Chancellor at the recommendation of the Prime Minister
Appointments of Supreme Court Justices are made by the Government at the recommendation of the Lord Chancellor

Appointments of Supreme Court Justices are made by the Supreme Court at the recommendation of the Prime Minister and Lord Chancellor, following the recommendation of an independent selection commission
Appointments of Supreme Court Justices are made by the Sovereign at the recommendation of the Prime Minister and Lord Chancellor, following the recommendation of an independent selection commission

Appointments of Supreme Court Justices are made by the Sovereign at the recommendation of the Prime Minister and Lord Chancellor, following the recommendation of an independent parliamentary select committee

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The appointment of Justices is made by the Sovereign at the recommendation of the Prime Minister and Lord Chancellor (a government minister), following the recommendation of an independent selection commission, consisting of that Court's President, Deputy President, and members of the judicial appointment commissions for the three judicial systems of the UK.

stem: Mr. Justice Holmes' nomination for appointment as a Justice of the Supreme Court is being considered by an independent selection commission. The Lord Chancellor has expressed his concern regarding Mr. Holmes' lack of judicial experience. The commission, nevertheless, has decided to approve the appointment of Mr. Justice Holmes as a Justice of the Supreme Court.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the powers of Lord Chancellor?

options.en: The Lord Chancellor must notify the Prime Minister of the name of the person selected
The Lord Chancellor may reject the selection on the grounds that, in the Lord Chancellor's opinion, Mr. Holmes is not suitable for the office concerned
The Lord Chancellor may reject Mr. Holmes' selection, as long as he informs the Sovereign of his reasons for doing so
The Lord Chancellor must orally order the commission to reconsider its selection if, in his opinion, Mr. Holmes in not suitable for the office concerned
The Lord Chancellor no longer has a role to play in the appointment of the judiciary since being replaced by the Lord Chief Justice as Head of the Judiciary of England and Wales

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. When a selection commission chooses a Supreme Court Justice, the Lord Chancellor may reject the selection on the grounds that, in his opinion, the person selected is not suitable for the office concerned. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 29 to the Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

stem: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council moved to the Supreme Court Building in Parliament Square in 2009. The Judicial Committee is the court of final appeal for the UK overseas territories and Crown dependencies, and for those Commonwealth countries that have retained the appeal to Her Majesty in Council or, in the case of Republics, to the Judicial Committee.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the role of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council?

options.en: Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are highly persuasive, but not binding on English courts
Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are binding on all English courts
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council no longer hears any appeals to Her Majesty in Council within the United Kingdom
Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are binding on all English courts below appellate level
The historic powers of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council within the United Kingdom are no longer governed by any domestic legislation

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are highly persuasive, but not binding on English courts. The Judicial Committee is a final court of appeal in civil and criminal matters from the courts of some Commonwealth countries and Colonial territories. As such it has no binding authority upon UK courts but is considered as very persuasive.

stem: The principles the Judicial Appointments Commission (JAC) will adopt in determining good character are based on: the overriding need to maintain public confidence in the standards of the judiciary; and the fact that public confidence will only be maintained if judicial office holders and those who aspire to such office maintain the highest standards of behaviour in their professional, public and private lives.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the eligibility requirement for the appointment of judges in England and Wales?

options.en: A potential High Court Judge must satisfy the judicial-appointment eligibility condition on a ten year basis
A potential Circuit Judges must satisfy the judicial-appointment eligibility condition on a ten year basis
A potential Master or Registrar must satisfy the judicial-appointment eligibility condition on a seven year basis
A potential District Judge must satisfy the judicial-appointment eligibility condition, on a five-year basis
It is mandatory that someone applying to become a judge of the Supreme Court to have previous judicial experience

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A potential District Judge (both County and Magistrates' Courts) must satisfy the judicial-appointment eligibility condition, on a five-year basis. The statutory qualification is a five-year right of audience - the right of a lawyer to appear and speak as an advocate for a party in a case in the court - in relation to all proceedings in any part of the Supreme Court, or all proceedings in county courts or magistrates' courts.

stem: There are over 500 District Judges, all of whom are appointed by Royal Warrant. The Bench covers seven regions: London, Midlands, North Eastern, Northern, South Eastern, Western and Wales.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the characteristics of District Judges?

options.en: District Judges sit in the County Court, the Magistrates' Court and the Crown court
District judges are part-time judges who deal with the majority of cases in the County court
District judges are full-time judges who deal with the majority of cases in the Crown court
District judges are full-time judges who deal with the majority of cases in the County court
District judges are appointed by the Queen, following a fair and open competition administered by the Lord Chancellor

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. District judges are full-time judges who deal with the majority of cases in the county courts. District judges are not sitting in the Crown courts. They are appointed by the Queen, following a fair and open competition administered by Judicial Appointments Commission.

stem: In Parliament debate a Member of Parliament (MP) from the opposition names a Government minister who (as believed by the MP) has breached his duties as a minister and therefore should be removed from office. The Minister, who obviously opposes the accusations of the MP, wishes to commence a claim against the MP on defamation.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The MP has an absolute protection from defamation claims
The MP has an absolute protection from defamation claims, however not on matters involving breach of his duties as a minister
The MP has a partial protection from defamation claims, however not on matters involving breach of his duties as a minister
The MP has a partial protection from defamation claims; in this case it is likely that the court will protect the MP
The MP has a partial protection from defamation claims; however, in this case it is likely that the court will not protect the MP

explanation.en: The best answer is D. The MP has a partial protection from defamation claims; in this case it is likely that the court will protect the MP. Parliamentary privilege has two heads (i) Freedom of speech, guaranteed by Article 9 of the Bill of Rights 1689. (II) Parliamentary control over its own affairs, or 'exclusive cognisance'. Whatever is said in debate in either chamber of Parliament is protected by the privilege of freedom of speech. Article 9 states: "That the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament." Parliamentary Privilege, however, does not, provide MPs with absolute protection (see R v Chaytor and others [2010] UKSC 52). In this case, however, it seems that the statement made by the MP is legitimate as it criticises the actions of the Government, which is one of the main roles of the opposition. Therefore, although parliamentary privilege is not an absolute right, it is likely that the court will protect the MP from a defamation claim.

stem: You arrive at the police station and hear that the officers are uncertain whether to charge your client with violent disorder or riot. There were 12 people present at the time.
ask: Which of the following is the most likely reason that the police would be considering violent disorder as opposed to riot?

options.en: If the police charge your client with riot they could be liable for compensation to members of the public
There was no actual violence
The smaller groups happened to come together and had not planned to come together
There were no members of the public present
There were no weapons being held

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. It is rare for the police to use section 1 riot as this can result in the police being regarded as having failed in their duties and therefore could be liable for compensation.

stem: A client of yours has been charged with riot and has been told that he will be required to surrender his passport.
ask: Which of the following is the most likely reason for a charge of riot to result in passports being surrendered?

options.en: There is a fear that the client will skip bail
The defendant is not a British national
The defendant has refused to identify himself
The riot was related to football hooliganism and there are international matches scheduled
The defendant was part of a recognised international gang

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The police have the power to insist on surrendering passports where football riots are in question in order to prevent the individuals travelling to international matches. This was brought in by the Football (Disorder) Act 2000 as a result of the difficulties in Euro 2000.

stem: Your client has been charged for a public order offence where he and 3 other persons had together made the public fear for their safety, although no actual physical action was undertaken.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate description of the charge being faced by your client?

options.en: Riot
Riot with intent
Violent disorder
Violent disorder with intent
Affray

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Violent disorder is the charge, for which there is a requirement for at least three persons to use or threaten unlawful violence together. As there are less than 12 people it could not be a riot and there was no physical action therefore it could not be affray (there must be some conduct, beyond the use of words, which is threatening and directed towards a person or persons to establish the affray offence). There is no such offence of 'with intent'.

stem: A client of yours has been arrested for affray and tells you that he was part of a group of four people, all of whom were shouting in an aggressive manner towards another person. There were no other members of the public present. You feel that your client has been charged with the wrong offence.
ask: Which of the following is the main reason for your belief?

options.en: There were more than three people present so must be violent disorder
The threats were by words alone so cannot be affray
There were no members of the public present so cannot be affray
There is a suggestion that the client himself was not the worst member of the group
The action was in private, not in public

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Unlike with riot and violent disorder when it comes to affray words are insufficient. The actions of the group as a collective will be considered and there can be 2 or more people. The threatening behaviour must cause a hypothetical bystander of reasonable firmness to fear for their safety, but no bystander need actually be present. There must, though, be a person present against whom the threatening behaviour is directed.

stem: Having put in details of an intended procession the police have given your client several restrictions. Your client is annoyed by the restrictions and asks you on what grounds the police can potentially restrict the procession.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate response to the query?

options.en: The issue being supported by the procession is thought to be politically incorrect
The procession is likely to seriously disrupt the community going to and from the local schools
There is a danger that someone may get injured
There is a likelihood that some individuals may not act in an orderly manner
The police don't have sufficient staff available on that day

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Only serious disruption, serious danger of criminal damage or serious likelihood of public disorder is sufficient for the police to place restrictions.

stem: m Having attempted to organise a procession and determining that it would be too difficult to move around the area without seriously disrupting the community, your client is now looking to have an assembly in one location. The client asks you what type of restrictions could be placed on assemblies.
ask: Which of the following would not be an acceptable restriction?

options.en: The location of the assembly
The maximum length of time for the assembly
The maximum number of people who can take part
The subject matter being discussed by the assembly
Restricting parking in the area

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The subject matter cannot as a matter of public law be subject to restriction (there are other laws in place to prevent racial hatred for example). Parking restrictions aren't expressly mentioned in Section 14 but the police have general powers to do this to ensure that there isn't unnecessary disruption.

stem: A colleague of yours is dealing with a client who has allegedly behaved in a way that is thought to be inciting racial hatred. You are asked for advice on how stirring up racial hatred is different to the general offences of intentional harassment.
ask: Which of these is the best answer to the question posed by your colleague?

options.en: The Attorney-General decides if proceedings should be instituted in offenses of racial hatred
The Chief Police Officer decides if proceedings should be instituted in offenses of racial hatred
The Chief Police Officer needs to be involved in the prosecution decisions
The local authority needs to give permission for the proceedings
The Attorney-General decides if proceedings should be instituted in offenses of intentional harassment

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The Attorney General is the individual to determine whether proceedings should be initiated.

stem: A colleague of yours rarely deals with the area of public order and the last case he dealt with was in 2004. He asks you what change have happened since 2004.
ask: Which of these would be the most important thing to mention to your colleague?

options.en: There has been increasing public concern about public order issues
Religious hatred is a new offence linked to racial hatred
The government is getting more involved in making public order decisions
Prison sentences have become less common as prisons are full
Courts have become more lenient for protesting and public order generally

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. In 2006 the Racial and Religious Hatred Act was enacted which brought in to deal with individuals who were intended to stir up religious hatred.

stem: A client of yours has been arrested for their part in a violent demonstration and is arguing that it is a breach of his human rights.
ask: Without considering the merits of his case what is the most accurate response to the client's immediate concern in relation to human rights?

options.en: This is a UK law issue so the European convention is irrelevant
Consideration needs to be given to the Human Rights Act 1998 but not the European convention
Human rights are irrelevant in this case
Consideration needs to be given to the right to peaceful assembly and the actions of the police
He has the right to protest and therefore he should not have been arrested

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Article 11 of the European Convention (which is also part of the Human Rights Act 1998) states that individuals have the right to a peaceful assembly, this does not automatically mean that they can't be arrested but it does mean that consideration needs to be given to balancing the two sides.

stem: The police have been informed that a group of 10 people are planning to march together towards Hyde Park, in London. The group intends to hand in a petition against the recent announcement by the Mayor of the City of London to prohibit cars from entering the City on Sundays. The police want to impose restrictions on this march.
ask: What advice would you give the police?

options.en: This is not a public procession, as there are less than 20 people participating; therefore, the police cannot impose any conditions
This is not a public procession, as there are less than 20 people participating; however, the police can still impose conditions and could even have the march banned
This is a public procession and the police can impose conditions on the march; however, they cannot have it banned
This is a public procession and the police can impose conditions on the march and, in certain cases, also have it banned
This is a public procession, as more than 2 people are attending it, and the police can impose conditions on the march and, in certain cases, also have it banned

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. This is a public procession and the police can impose conditions on the march and, in certain cases, also have it banned. In Flockhart v Robinson [1950], it was stated that "... a procession was more than "a mere body of persons;..it is a body of persons who are moving along a route". The law does not provide a minimum number to constitute a procession, so, even a small number of people will constitute a procession. The police may impose conditions on processions and, in limited circumstances, have the processions banned.

stem: Mr. Backfield has notified the police, in writing, about his intention to organise a route for a procession towards the City of London, in order to protest against future real estate tax increases. The written notice specified a date scheduled for the 12th calendar day of the following month, at 10.00am. It also included the contact details of Mr. Backfield and the proposed route of the procession. The procession, however, eventually began at 3.00pm instead of 10.00am and caused considerable interference, as more participants attended the event than were initially expected. The police have charged Mr. Backfield, due to his failure to comply with the provisions of the Public Order Act 1986.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: As the Organiser of a public procession, Mr. Backfield did not give sufficient notice to the police. His failure to comply with the provisions of the Act is a criminal offence
As the Organiser of a public procession, Mr. Backfield did not give sufficient notice to the police; however, it is a defence for him to show that the procession diverged from the notified time
As the Organiser of a public procession, Mr. Backfield did give sufficient notice to the police; however, the fact that the procession diverged from the notified time is not a defence for him

As the Organiser of a public procession, Mr. Backfield did give sufficient notice to the police; the fact that the procession diverged from the notified time can be a defence for him, in certain circumstances

As the Organiser of a public procession, Mr. Backfield did not give sufficient notice to the police; however, it is a defence for him to show that he did know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Public processions require that the police are given at least 6 clear days' written notice (if that is not reasonably practicable, as soon as delivery is reasonably practicable) of the date, time, proposed route and the name and address of at least one person proposing to organise the procession, known as the "Organiser". It is a defence to a charge to show that the "Organiser" did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice, or the difference of date, time or route. The difficulties inherent in establishing the negatives involved in the defences are apparent. It is also a defence for an "Organiser", who is being prosecuted, to prove that the difference arose from circumstances beyond his control.

stem: Mr. Blue organised a public procession in one of the main streets, in Liverpool, due to the intention of the local football club to trade one of its leading players. Mr. Blue did not give any written notice to the police about the event. The police filed criminal charges against Mr. Blue for failure to comply with the requirement to give advanced written notice, in accordance with the Public Order Act 1986.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal situation?

options.en: It is not a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice
It is a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice
It is not a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice
It is a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice

It is a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice; this defence can only stand if there is only one organiser of a public procession

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. As the organiser of the public procession, Mr Blue is required by law to give written advance notice of the public procession to a police station not less than 6 clear days before the date when the procession is intended to be held, unless it is not reasonably practicable to give any advance notice of the procession. However such notice was not given by Mr Blue. It would be, however, a defence to the charge for Mr. Blue to show that he did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice (see section 11(8) of the Public Order Act 1986).

stem: Ten students from the local university are planning to demonstrate next to a building which is part of the Finance Department of the university, due to the recent announcement by the university to double the parking charges in the university's car park. The senior manager of the Finance Department, who is aware of this intention, called the police and asked them to take steps to prevent this event from happening.
ask: What would you advise the police?

options.en: This is a public assembly. There is no requirement to give prior notice of an assembly. The police, however, can impose conditions and ban the event, if it could, potentially, cause serious public disorder, serious criminal damage, or serious disruption to the life of the community
This is not a public assembly, as there are less than 20 people attending. The police cannot impose any conditions, nor ban the event

This is a public assembly. There is no requirement to give prior notice of an assembly. The police, however, can impose conditions, but cannot ban the event, even if it has the potential to cause serious public disorder, serious criminal damage, or serious disruption to the life of the community
This is not a public assembly, as the event which is about to take place is in the open air

This is a public assembly. There is a requirement to give prior notice of an assembly to the police. The police, however, can impose conditions or ban the event, even if it has the potential to cause serious public disorder, serious criminal damage, or serious disruption to the life of the community

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Public assembly means an assembly of 2 or more persons, in a public place, which is wholly or partly open to the air. Unlike public processions, there is no requirement to give prior notice of an assembly; however, under the Public Order Act, the police do have specific powers to control assemblies. The Act provides police with the power to impose conditions on assemblies, in order "...to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage, or serious disruption to the life of the community".

stem: The police have been informed about a public assembly that will take place, next week, adjacent to the City Hall. The police are concerned that, following the event, it may cause serious public disorder and public damage and serious disruption to the life of the community. The police have, therefore, imposed a few conditions on the event: a) that the assembly will only take place at the weekend; b) that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30; c) that the event will only take place at the rear of the City Hall; and d) that it will not last more than 2 hours.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the powers of the police to impose conditions on the public assembly?

options.en: The police can impose such conditions that the assembly will only take place, at the weekend; that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30; and that the event will only take place, at the rear of the City Hall; but the police cannot limit the event to last for less than 2 hours

The police can impose such conditions that the assembly will only take place at the weekend; that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30; and that the event will not last for more than 2 hours; but they cannot impose such a condition that it will only take place at the rear of the City Hall

The police can impose such conditions that the assembly will only take place at the weekend; it will only take place, at the rear of the City Hall; that it will not last for more than 2 hours; the police cannot, however, impose such a condition that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30

The police can impose such conditions that the assembly will only take place, at the rear of the City Hall; that it will not last for more than 2 hours; and that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30; the police, however, cannot impose such a condition that the assembly will only take place at the weekend

The police can impose such conditions that the assembly can only take place at the weekend, and that the number of people who may take part will not exceed 30. It cannot, however, impose such conditions that the assembly will not last for more than 2 hours, nor that it will only take place, at the rear of the City Hall

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Section 14 of the Public Order Act 1986 provides the police with the power to impose conditions on assemblies: "to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community"; however, the conditions are limited to the specifying of the number of people who may take part; the location of the assembly; and its maximum duration. The police, therefore, cannot impose a condition as to the day of the event.

stem: Caroline and two friends take part in a procession through their local town. Caroline is arrested under the Public Order Act 1986 for failure to give adequate notice. She claims that as only three people took part there was no requirement to give notice.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Notice must only be given when six or more people take part in a procession
There is no minimum requirement for the number of people taking part in a procession and thus notice is required regardless of the number of attendees
Notice must only be given when 12 or more people take part in the procession
Notice must only be given when 100 or more people take part in the procession
There is no requirement to give notice of a procession regardless of the number of people taking part

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. There is no minimum number of participants to constitute a procession. Public processions are required to give at least 6 clear days' written notice (if that is not reasonably practicable, as soon as delivery is reasonably practicable) of notice of the date, time, proposed route and the name and address of at least one person proposing to organise it, known as the "Organiser".

stem: Carol decides to organise a public procession and informs the police. However, the Chief Police Officer feels the nature of the procession is inappropriate and applies to the local authority for a banning order. Carol believes she has the right to conduct the procession regardless.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal situation?

options.en: A public procession cannot be banned or have conditions imposed
A public procession can have conditions imposed but cannot be banned
Providing the Chief Police Officer applied to the local authority and seeks confirmation from the Home Secretary, a procession can be banned
A Chief Police Officer has the authority to ban the procession without seeking further confirmation
A Chief Police Officer only requires support from the local authority to ban a procession

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. If a Chief Police Officer applies to the local authority and seeks confirmation from the Home Secretary, a public procession can be banned under the Public Order Act 1986.

stem: A public assembly is due to be held in the town centre. Police impose conditions limiting the maximum duration and location. Organisers are unhappy and claim the police aren't entitled to impose such limits.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe the legal position?

options.en: No limits can be imposed on assemblies. Limits can only be imposed on public processions
Although limits can be imposed on assemblies, police cannot limit maximum duration
Although limits can be imposed on assemblies, police cannot specify the location
Police can either limit the duration or location but not both in relation to the same assembly
Police are within their rights to limit the location and duration in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The Public Order Act 1986 gives police the right to limit the location, maximum duration and the number of people who take part in an assembly in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community.

stem: Sebastian arranges a public assembly and hopes that over 500 people will attend. However, police limit the number of attendees to 200. Sebastian wants to know if they are allowed to do this.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe the legal position?

options.en: Police can limit the number of attendees only
Police can limit the number of attendees and the duration only
Police can limit the number of attendees and the location
Police can limit the number of attendees, the location and the duration
Police can limit the location and duration only

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The Public Order Act 1986 gives police the right to limit the location, maximum duration and the number of people who take part in an assembly in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community. any impact on your learning or

stem: James wants to arrange a public assembly but is unsure what rights he has and what rights the police have in regulating public assemblies.
ask: Which of the following statements best describe the legal position?

options.en: Police cannot impose any conditions on assemblies
Police can impose any conditions they wish on assemblies
Police can impose limited conditions on assemblies if they see fit

Police can impose limited conditions, including the maximum number of attendees, on assemblies in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community
Police cannot impose conditions but can ban assemblies in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. According to the Public Order Act 1986 police have the right to limit the location, maximum duration and the number of people who take part in an assembly in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community.

stem: Angela wishes to organise a public assembly in the local town. Police then inform her that they will be imposing conditions in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community. The conditions state that the assembly must be held in a side street 3 miles out of town, with no more than three attendees for a maximum duration of twelve minutes. Angela argues that it is breach of her right to assembly under Art. 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The police officers can impose any conditions they see fit in order to prevent serious public disorder, serious criminal damage or serious disruption to the life of the community and Angela has no recourse
The police have merely asserted their right to limit the duration, location and number of attendees and Angela has no recourse
The conditions can be argued to be excessive and are likely to violate Art. 11 under the Convention
The police officers can impose any conditions they see fit in order to prevent serious public disorder only
Art. 11 doesn't give a right to a public assembly

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. If conditions are so strict they stop the assembly from taking place in a meaningful way they may constitute an unlawful ban. Furthermore, they may infringe the rights given under Art. 11 (right to assembly).

stem: Peter and four friends are taking part in a small protest. The situation becomes heated and they are arrested rioting. Peter and his friends argue that they cannot possibly be guilty of the offence as there were only eleven people taking part in the protest.
ask: With reference to the Public Order Act 1986 (the Act), which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: It is irrelevant how many people took part in the protest
The Act states that there must be a minimum of three people to constitute the offence of rioting, so Peter and his friends could be charged if they have committed the other elements of the offence
The Act states that there must be a minimum of seven people to constitute the offence of rioting, so Peter and his friends could be charged if they have committed the other elements of the offence

The Act states that there must be a minimum of twelve people to constitute the offence of rioting, so Peter and his friends could not be lawfully charged even if they have committed the other elements of the offence

The Act states that there must be a minimum of one hundred people to constitute the offence of rioting, so Peter and his friends could not be lawfully charged even if they have committed the other elements of the offence

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. According to the Public Order Act 1986 'twelve or more persons present together' will constitute the offence of riot (providing the other elements of the offence have been satisfied). However, if there are fewer than twelve persons present the Public Order Act 1986 does list other offences that they may be charged with.

stem: Brian and Andy are arrested for violent disorder. They claim that they cannot be liable for the offence because there are only two of them.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: A person can be guilty of violent disorder when acting alone
At least two or more people must be present to constitute the offence of violent disorder
At least three or more people must be present to constitute the offence of violent disorder
At least twelve or more people must be present to constitute the offence of violent disorder
At least one hundred or more people must be present to constitute the offence of violent disorder

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. At least three or more people must be present to be liable for the offence of violent disorder under the Public Order Act 1986.

stem: John, Rob and Chris have been arrested for violent disorder. They argue that they can't have committed the offence because they were on private land at the time the alleged offence took place.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The offence can be committed on private as well as public land
The offence can only be committed on public land
The offence can only be committed on private land
The offence can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by a business
The offence can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by an individual

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Under the Public Order Act 1986 the offence can be committed on public and private land.

stem: Sean, amongst others, has been arrested for violent disorder. He claims that he did not intend or was aware that his behaviour could be constituted as violence or as threatening violence.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: His intent is irrelevant
The fact is was unaware that his behaviour could be seen as threatening violence is irrelevant
In order to be liable he must have intended violence or intended to threaten violence
In order to be liable he must have intended violence or intended to threaten violence or be aware that his conduct may be interpreted as being violent or threatening violence
His state of mind during the offence is irrelevant

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Under the Public Order Act 1986 a person will only be guilty of violent disorder if they intend to use or threaten violence or are aware that their conduct may be violent or threaten violence

stem: Scott and Oliver have been arrested for affray following an argument at a nightclub. Although Scott used threatening language he argues that they cannot be guilty of affray as their conduct wasn't threatening.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Conduct is irrelevant in relation to the offence of affray
Words alone can constitute enough of a threat to be liable for affray
Words alone cannot constitute affray. Conduct must also be taken into account
Whether or not conduct is relevant is left to the discretion of the police
Whether or not conduct is relevant is left to the discretion of the judge

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The Public Order Act 1986 states that a person will be guilty of affray if 'he uses or threatens unlawful violence towards another and his conduct is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety'. It is evident, therefore, that in addition to other elements, conduct is relevant to potential liability for the offence of affray.

stem: A man has been arrested for fighting another person in a pub and is charged with affray. A woman who is present at the scene is put in substantial fear for her safety, although the fighting is not directed towards her.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The man has committed the offence of affray
The man has committed the offence of affray against the other person he was fighting with
The man has not committed the offence of affray as it can only be established when two or more persons commit the offence
The man has not committed the offence of affray as it can only be established when seven or more persons commit the offence
The man has not committed the offence of affray as it can only be established when twelve or more persons commit the offence

explanation.en: The best answer is A. The man has committed the offence of affray. Affray is the fighting of two or more persons in a public or private place, in a way that would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety. According to section 3(1) of the Public Order Act 1986, a person is guilty of affray if he uses or threatens unlawful violence towards another and his conduct is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his personal safety. A person is guilty of affray only if he intends to use or threaten violence, or is aware that his conduct may be violent, or threaten violence. Section 3(2) states that where 2 or more persons use or threaten the unlawful violence, it is the conduct of them taken together that must be considered for the purposes of section 3 (1). However, the offence of affray can be committed by one person only. The test established in R v Sanchez [1996] Crim LR 572 CA requires that the hypothetical bystander (in this case the woman), rather than the victim, must be put in fear for his or her personal safety. Apart from the hypothetical bystander, there must be a 'victim' present (i.e., the other person the man was fighting with) against whom the violence is to be directed (I & Others v DPP [2002] 1 AC 285 HL). Where the violence is focused solely and exclusively on the victim, such that it would be incapable of causing a person of reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his safety, then the offence is not made out (Leeson v DPP [2010] EWHC 994 (Admin)). Hence, option is incorrect.

stem: Harry is arrested under s4 Public Order Act 1986 after holding up a sign with offensive content in the middle of the town. Harry argues that he cannot be guilty because he did not vocalise the content.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: A sign cannot constitute an offence
