A sign can only constitute an offence if it is accompanied by actual violence
A sign can only constitute an offence if it is accompanied by actual or threatened violence
A sign can only constitute an offence if it is accompanied by violence or threatened violence as determined by conduct and/or words
A sign alone can constitute an offence

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. S4 of the Public Order Act 1986 states that a person will be guilty if they ' distribute or display to another person any writing, sign or other visible representation which is threatening, abusive or insulting, with intent to cause that person to believe that immediate unlawful violence will be used against him or another by any person, or to provoke the immediate use of unlawful violence by that person or another, or whereby that person is likely to believe that such violence will be used, or it is likely that such violence will be provoked.

stem: When out walking Peter starts to shout at Adam using threatening and abusive words causing Adam distress. Peter is later arrested under S4A Public Order Act 1986 (fear or provocation of violence) but claims he cannot be liable due to the fact they were on private land at the time of the alleged offence.
ask: Advise Peter if he is correct regarding his liability?

options.en: The offence can be committed on private as well as public land
The offence can only be committed on public land
The offence can only be committed on private land
The offence can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by a business
The offence can be committed on private land but only if the land is owned by an individual

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Under the Public Order Act 1986, the offence of fear or provocation of violence can be committed on public or private land (but not if both parties are in a dwelling).

stem: Beth decides to go on to private land but is directed away from the land by police. Believing trespass is not a criminal offence she decides to ignore their directions and goes on to the land anyway. She has now been arrested for aggravated trespass.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Any form of trespass is a civil wrong
A person cannot be arrested for any form of trespass
Failure to follow directions does not form part of an offence
Failure to comply with directions away from private land can constitute an offence
Aggravated trespass only applies to Crown land

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Under the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 it can constitute an offence if you fail to comply with directions or return to the land within 3 months of such directions being issued.

stem: Police hear of a rave which has been organised without the landowner's permission. The Chief Police Officer applies to the local council in order to prohibit the trespassory assembly. They visit the site and direct attendees away from the site. Hannah and Lauren ignore the directions and proceed on to the land.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: They have not committed a criminal offence by ignoring the directions
They have not committed a criminal offence by ignoring the directions unless they are violent when on the land
They have committed a criminal offence by ignoring the directions
They have only committed a civil wrong by going on the land
They have only committed a civil wrong by ignoring the directions

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Under the Public Order Act 1986 if anyone who knows of the order organises or participates in the trespassory assembly it will constitute an offence. To ignore the instructions not to proceed is also an offence.

stem: Owen and Max decide to demonstrate at Windsor Castle. They are arrested for trespass on a designated site. They are confused as they thought trespass was a civil wrong.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Any form of trespass is purely a civil wrong
Trespass on a designated site is an offence but Crown land does not constitute a designated site
Trespass on a designated site is an offence and Crown land does constitute a designated site
Trespass on a designated site is an offence but a person is only liable if violent when on the land
Trespass on a designated site is an offence but a person is only liable if violent or intimidating when on the land

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005 created the offence of trespass on designated land. However, in addition to Crown land, this section also allows the Secretary of State to designate any other site which he considers appropriate to designate, in the interests of national security.

stem: Phoebe organised a procession and gave notice to police. Unknown to her, another organiser delayed the start of the procession by one hour. She is now fearful that she has committed an offence by not informing police of the change.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: Phoebe has no defence and could be charged with an offence
She is under no obligation to provide any notice to police
She has the defence that she was unaware, nor suspected or had reason to suspect the change in timings
Phoebe is only obligated to inform police of the location of the procession
Phoebe is only obligated to inform police of the date of the procession

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The Public Order Act 1986 provides a defence if the organiser did not know of, and neither suspected, nor had reason to suspect, the failure to satisfy the requirements of notice, or the difference of date, time or route.

stem: Millie is asked to help steward a procession. Unknown to her, police have not been given notice and she is held accountable as an organiser. Millie claims that she is merely a steward and is not connected to the organisation of the event.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: As a steward technically Millie is an organiser
As a steward Millie would not be considered an organiser unless she had helped plan the event in advance
As a steward Millie would not be considered an organiser unless she had helped plan the event in advance and had written confirmation of her status as organiser
The organiser had not obligation to inform police
The organiser has not committed a crime by failing to inform the police

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. 'Organiser' is not defined in the statute, and although Flockhart v Robinson [1950] may have implied that those who direct the route are organisers. It is generally accepted that it is the advance planning of a procession that indicates who is the organiser.

stem: A police officer had counted 21 people on a roadside verge adjacent to the perimeter fence of Stonehenge, despite an order being in force banning assemblies of 20 people or more. The officer told them that they constituted a trespassory assembly and asked them to move off. Some, including Keith, had remained and been arrested.
ask: Did Keith's use of the road constitute a trespass?

options.en: No, because the law recognises that the public highway is a public place on which all manner of reasonable activities might go on
No, because the common law allows virtually unlimited freedom on the public's right of user of the highway
Yes, there is a criminal offence of "trespassory assembly", which is aimed at curbing protests on public roads

Yes, because there is a limited right to assemble freely in a public place if the police seek and obtain a banning order from a local authority under on the grounds that there is danger of disruption to the life of the community

Yes, because the public's right of access to the highway is limited to the right to pass and re-pass and to do anything incidental or ancillary to that right, and peaceful assembly is not so incidental

explanation.en: A is correct. As long as Keith's activities were reasonable, did not involve the commission of a public or private nuisance and did not amount to an obstruction of the highway unreasonably impeding the primary right of the general public to pass and re-pass, they should not constitute a trespass. Lead case: DPP v Jones [1999] 2 AC 240, [1999] 2 All ER 257.
